13724.e: Lucy belongs to the species Australopithecus afarensis and lived about 3.2 million years ago. About 40 per cent of her skeleton has been preserved.
13724.m: Lucy is one of the most famous fossils of early hominins.

13725.q: Which ability did human ancestors develop very early, even before the brain grew much bigger?
13725.e: Even early hominins such as Lucy walked upright. But for a long time their brains stayed about as big as those of apes.
13725.m: Walking upright came before the big brain.

13726.q: What do the footprints of Laetoli in Tanzania, about 3.6 million years old, show?
a: That early hominins already walked upright
That there were horses at that time
13726.e: The prints were pressed into volcanic ash and turned to stone. They were probably made by Australopithecus afarensis.
13726.m: The Laetoli footprints prove that walking upright began early.

13727.q: What does the name “Homo habilis” mean?
13727.e: Homo habilis lived about 2.1 to 1.5 million years ago in Africa. It got its name because the simple stone tools found in the same layers were thought to be its work.

13728.q: Which human species was one of the first to leave Africa and spread as far as Asia?
13728.e: Homo erectus, the “upright man”, reached Georgia almost 2 million years ago and later China and Indonesia.
13728.m: Homo erectus was one of the first humans outside Africa.

13729.q: Which typical stone tool is closely linked to Homo erectus?
13729.e: The hand axe is a stone worked on both sides that had many uses. It was made for more than a million years.
13729.m: The hand axe is an all-purpose tool of the Old Stone Age.

13730.q: Why was using fire important for early humans?
a: Warmth, protection and cooked food that was easier to digest
13730.e: Fire protected against cold and predators. Cooked food provided more energy, which may have helped the brain to grow.
13730.m: Fire greatly changed the lives of early humans.

13731.q: What is the oldest and longest period of human history, which began with the first stone tools, called?
13731.e: The Old Stone Age began about 2.6 million years ago with the first stone tools. It only ended about 12,000 years ago.
13731.m: The Old Stone Age is the longest period of human history.

13732.q: Which small human species was discovered on an Indonesian island in 2003 and nicknamed the “hobbit”?
13732.e: Homo floresiensis lived on the island of Flores and was only about one metre tall. The species shows that several human species once lived at the same time.
13732.m: Homo floresiensis was a small human species on Flores.

13733.q: Where does the Neanderthal get its name from?
a: From a valley near Düsseldorf where bones were found in 1856
From a scientist called Neander who dug it up
From a Greek word for giant
13733.e: In 1856, workers discovered bones in a cave in the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf. The valley itself was named after the hymn writer Joachim Neander.
13733.m: The Neanderthal is named after a valley near Düsseldorf.

13734.q: In which area did the Neanderthals live?
a: In Europe and in West and Central Asia
13734.e: Neanderthals lived in Europe and further east as far as Central Asia. They were well adapted to the cold climate of the ice ages.
13734.m: The Neanderthals lived in Europe and West Asia.

13735.q: Roughly how long ago did the Neanderthals die out?
13735.e: The most recent reliably dated Neanderthal finds are about 40,000 years old. At about this time, Homo sapiens was spreading through Europe.
13735.m: The Neanderthals disappeared about 40,000 years ago.

13736.q: What physical features did Neanderthals have compared with people today?
a: A stocky, strong build with heavy brow ridges
Very long, thin arms and legs
A much smaller brain than a chimpanzee
Fur all over the body like a bear
13736.e: The compact, muscular body helped keep in heat in the cold climate. The ridges above the eyes and the large nose were also striking.
13736.m: Neanderthals were strongly built and adapted to the cold.

13737.q: How big was the Neanderthal brain compared with that of people today?
a: On average about the same size or a little bigger
Only as big as a fist
13737.e: On average, Neanderthals had a brain volume similar to or slightly larger than people today. But a big brain alone does not automatically mean higher intelligence.

13738.q: In which caves in Appenzell Innerrhoden did Emil Bächler find traces of Neanderthals from 1904 onwards?
13738.e: In the caves below the Ebenalp in the Alpstein, Emil Bächler found worked stones and bones. They show that Neanderthals lived in the Alpstein, and the caves were also used by cave bears as winter quarters.
13738.m: Traces of Neanderthals in the Alps were found in the Wildkirchli.

13739.e: Neanderthals shaped stones carefully. This produced sharp scrapers and points for spears.

13740.q: What have genetic researchers found out about Neanderthals and people today?
a: Many people today carry one to two per cent Neanderthal DNA
Neanderthals are the direct ancestors of all Europeans
Neanderthals had no DNA at all
Neanderthals and Homo sapiens are not related
13740.e: Neanderthals and Homo sapiens had children together. That is why the DNA of people outside Africa contains a small share of Neanderthal DNA.
13740.m: Many people today carry some Neanderthal DNA.

13741.q: What did the scientist Svante Pääbo obtain from old Neanderthal bones?
13741.e: Svante Pääbo decoded the Neanderthal genome. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2022.
13741.m: Svante Pääbo decoded the Neanderthal genome.

13742.q: Which group of humans related to the Neanderthals was discovered mainly through DNA from a finger bone in a Siberian cave?
13742.e: In 2008, a small finger bone was found in the Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains. Its DNA revealed a group of humans unknown until then.
13742.m: The Denisovans were discovered mainly through their DNA.

13743.q: Which clues show that Neanderthals were not as primitive as people long thought?
a: They used fire, sometimes buried their dead and cared for the sick
They kept farm animals such as cows
13743.e: Finds show that Neanderthals could control fire, fixed tools to handles with birch tar and looked after injured members of their group. Some of the dead were buried on purpose.
13743.m: Neanderthals were skilful and social people.

13744.q: Which large animal, among others, did Neanderthals hunt in the Ice Age?
13744.e: Neanderthals were successful hunters and killed animals such as reindeer, wild horses, bison and sometimes mammoths. They used wooden spears and stone points to do so.
13744.m: Neanderthals hunted large Ice Age animals.

13745.q: What does the Latin name “Homo sapiens” mean?
13745.e: The Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus gave humans this scientific name in 1758. “Sapiens” is Latin and means “wise” or “knowing”.

13746.q: How old are the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco?
13746.e: The finds from Jebel Irhoud were dated in 2017 to about 300,000 years. They show that our species lived in Africa very early on.
13746.m: Homo sapiens has existed for about 300,000 years.

13747.q: What is the theory called that Homo sapiens developed in Africa and spread from there around the world?
13747.e: According to the Out of Africa theory, groups of Homo sapiens left Africa mainly about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago. Genetic studies support this theory.

13748.q: According to current knowledge, how did people first reach America?
a: Over a land bridge or along the coast between Siberia and Alaska
By ship across the Atlantic from Europe
Over a land bridge from Africa to Brazil
13748.e: In the Ice Age the sea level was lower, and Siberia and Alaska were joined by the land bridge Beringia. People reached America this way at least about 15,000 years ago.
13748.m: The first people reached America via Beringia.

13749.q: What are the early Homo sapiens who lived in Europe in the Ice Age called, after a site in France?
13749.e: The name comes from the Cro-Magnon rock shelter in southern France, where skeletons were found in 1868. Cro-Magnon people belong to our own species.
13749.m: Cro-Magnon people were early Homo sapiens in Europe.

13750.q: In which French cave are there famous animal paintings more than 30,000 years old?
13750.e: Chauvet Cave was discovered in 1994 and contains pictures of lions, rhinos, horses and mammoths. They are among the oldest known cave paintings.
13750.m: Chauvet Cave shows very old art by Homo sapiens.

13751.q: Which famous engraving was found in the Kesslerloch near Thayngen (canton of Schaffhausen)?
13751.e: The engraving on a piece of reindeer antler was discovered in 1874 and today is also called the “Searching Reindeer”. It was made by people who used the Kesslerloch about 15,000 to 11,000 years ago.
13751.m: The “Grazing Reindeer” from the Kesslerloch is world-famous.

13752.q: How did people mainly live in the Old Stone Age?
13752.e: People followed the herds of animals and gathered plants, berries and roots. Permanent villages and farming only came in the New Stone Age.
13752.m: In the Old Stone Age, people lived as hunter-gatherers.

13753.q: What were the oldest known flutes, found in caves in the Swabian Jura, made from?
a: From bird bones and mammoth ivory
13753.e: In caves such as Geissenklösterle and Hohle Fels, flutes about 40,000 years old were found. They are among the oldest musical instruments in the world.
13753.m: People were already making music about 40,000 years ago.

13754.q: Which Old Stone Age hunting weapon increased the range and force of a spear?
a: The leather sling with lead balls
13754.e: With a spear-thrower, the arm works like a longer lever. Finely decorated spear-throwers made of reindeer antler are known mainly from France.
13754.m: The spear-thrower made spears faster and more dangerous.

13755.q: What was Switzerland like at the height of the last Ice Age, about 20,000 years ago?
a: Large parts were covered by glaciers
13755.e: In the last cold period, the Alpine glaciers reached far out into the Swiss Plateau. Only when the ice melted could people use Switzerland permanently again.
13755.m: In the last Ice Age, a large part of Switzerland was covered by glaciers.

13756.q: Which Ice Age ivory figure from the Swabian Jura shows a being with a human body and a lion's head?
13756.e: The Lion Man from the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave is about 40,000 years old. It is considered one of the oldest known works of art and shows the imagination of early humans.
13756.m: The Lion Man is one of the oldest works of art in the world.

13757.q: What did people in the Old Stone Age mainly make their tools from?
13757.e: People did not know about metals yet. Experts also call the Old Stone Age the Palaeolithic, from the Greek “palaios” for old and “lithos” for stone.
13757.m: In the Old Stone Age, tools were made of stone, bone and wood.

13758.q: Roughly when did the Old Stone Age begin?
13758.e: The Old Stone Age begins with the oldest known stone tools in Africa. These are more than 2.5 million years old.
13758.m: The Old Stone Age began more than two million years ago in Africa.

13759.q: Which part of the Stone Age lasted by far the longest?
13759.e: The Old Stone Age makes up well over 99 per cent of human history. The Middle and New Stone Ages together lasted only a few thousand years.
13759.m: The Old Stone Age is by far the longest period of human history.

13760.q: What is the period between the Old Stone Age and the New Stone Age called?
13760.e: The Middle Stone Age is called the Mesolithic by experts. During this time, people still lived as hunter-gatherers.
13760.m: The Middle Stone Age lies between the Old and New Stone Ages.

13761.q: Roughly what marked the end of the Old Stone Age in Europe?
a: The end of the last Ice Age
The building of the first towns
13761.e: The climate became much warmer, the glaciers melted and forests spread. This is when the Middle Stone Age begins in Europe.
13761.m: The Old Stone Age in Europe ended with the end of the last Ice Age.

13762.q: Which human species lived in Europe in the Old Stone Age before Homo sapiens arrived?
13762.e: The Neanderthal lived in Europe and West Asia long before Homo sapiens. It died out about 40,000 years ago.
13762.m: Before modern humans, the Neanderthal lived in Europe.

13763.q: Which cave in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden is known for finds from the Old Stone Age?
13763.e: In the Wildkirchli on the Ebenalp, stone tools and many cave bear bones were found. The cave is one of the best-known Old Stone Age sites in Switzerland.
13763.m: Traces of Old Stone Age people were found in the Wildkirchli.

13764.q: Which work of art was found in the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen SH?
13764.e: Towards the end of the last Ice Age, the Kesslerloch was a camp of reindeer hunters. The engraving of a reindeer on a piece of reindeer antler is famous; it used to be called the “Grazing Reindeer” and is now called the “Searching Reindeer”.
13764.m: The famous engraving of a reindeer was found in the Kesslerloch near Thayngen.

a: A small stone figure of a woman
A cave painting of a goddess
13765.e: The limestone figure, about 11 centimetres tall, was found in Austria in 1908. It is about 30,000 years old.
13765.m: The Venus of Willendorf is a small figure of a woman from the Old Stone Age.

13766.q: What is the technical term for the New Stone Age?
13766.e: “Neolithic” literally means “new stone age”. The term comes from Greek.
13766.m: The technical term for the New Stone Age is Neolithic.

13767.q: In which region did the New Stone Age begin first?
13767.e: In the Fertile Crescent in the Near East, people were the first to begin farming crops and keeping animals. The area stretches in an arc from what is now Israel through Syria to Iraq.
13767.m: The New Stone Age began in the Fertile Crescent.

13768.q: Around what time did the New Stone Age begin in the Near East?
13768.e: The first farmers lived about 11,500 years ago in the area of what is now Iraq, Syria and Turkey.
13768.m: The New Stone Age began in the Near East about 11,500 years ago.

13769.q: Roughly when did the farming way of life reach Central Europe?
13769.e: Farming spread slowly from the Near East to Europe. By around 5500 BC, the first farmers were also living in Central Europe.
13769.m: There were farmers in Central Europe from about 5500 BC.

13770.q: Which period followed the New Stone Age in Central Europe?
13770.e: Around 2200 BC, people in Central Europe began to make bronze from copper and tin. This ended the New Stone Age.
13770.m: The Bronze Age followed the New Stone Age.

13771.q: Which way of working stone was new in the New Stone Age?
13771.e: In the New Stone Age, stone axes were ground smooth and given a hole for the handle. That is why it is also called the “age of polished stone”.
13771.m: In the New Stone Age, people learned to grind and drill stones.

13772.q: When was the glacier mummy “Ötzi” found in the Ötztal Alps?
13772.e: Hikers discovered Ötzi in September 1991 at the Tisenjoch, at more than 3200 metres. Today he lies in the archaeology museum in Bolzano.
13772.m: Ötzi was found in 1991 in the ice of the Ötztal Alps.

13773.q: Roughly when did the “Iceman”, Ötzi, live?
13773.e: Ötzi died about 5300 years ago at the end of the New Stone Age. He already carried an axe with a copper blade.

13774.q: In which present-day country is the more than 11,000-year-old ritual site of Göbekli Tepe?
13774.e: Göbekli Tepe is in south-eastern Turkey, near the city of Şanlıurfa. The oldest large, decorated stone pillars were made around 9600 BC and are among the oldest known structures for worship and gatherings.
13774.m: Göbekli Tepe in Turkey is one of the oldest ritual sites in the world.

13775.q: Why did hunter-gatherers often move from place to place?
a: They followed animals and ripe plants
They were looking for metal for tools
They wanted to found new towns
13775.e: Food could be found in different places depending on the season. That is why the groups followed the herds of animals and the ripe fruit.
13775.m: Hunter-gatherers did not settle and followed their food.

13776.q: What do we call a way of life without a fixed home?
13776.e: Nomads regularly change where they live. The hunter-gatherers of the Stone Age lived a nomadic life.
13776.m: Anyone who moves around without a fixed home lives a nomadic life.

13777.q: Which animals did people in Ice Age Central Europe hunt especially often?
13777.e: Large herds of reindeer and wild horses lived on the cold Ice Age steppe. They provided meat, skins, bones and antlers.
13777.m: Reindeer and wild horses were important Ice Age prey.

13778.q: What was the spear-thrower used for?
a: To throw spears further and harder
To pull fish out of the water
13778.e: The spear-thrower lengthens the arm like a lever. This made the spear fly faster and further.
13778.m: With a spear-thrower, spears flew further and faster.

a: A rock overhang that gives shelter from the weather
A tent made of mammoth bones
A raft made of tree trunks
13779.e: Under an abri, an overhanging roof of rock, people were protected from rain and wind. Many Stone Age camps were under such rock shelters.
13779.m: An abri is a sheltering rock roof.

13780.q: How big were groups of hunter-gatherers usually?
13780.e: A group had to live from what the surrounding area provided. That is why usually only a few families lived together.

13781.q: What did reindeer hunters at the end of the Ice Age make harpoons from?
13781.e: Reindeer antler is hard and easy to carve. Barbed harpoons were used for fishing and hunting.
13781.m: Stone Age harpoons were often carved from antler.

13782.q: Which people in southern Africa traditionally lived as hunter-gatherers until fairly recent times?
13782.e: The San live in the Kalahari. Some of them lived as hunter-gatherers until the 20th century.
13782.m: The San in the Kalahari lived as hunter-gatherers for a long time.

13783.q: What, among other things, did hunter-gatherers gather?
13783.e: People knew many edible wild plants. Berries, nuts, mushrooms and roots added to the meat from hunting.
13783.m: Hunter-gatherers also ate berries, nuts and roots.

13784.q: What did the glaciers of the last Ice Age leave behind on the Swiss Plateau?
13784.e: The glaciers carried boulders from the Alps far out onto the Swiss Plateau. When the ice melted, these erratics were left behind.
13784.m: Erratics are boulders that glaciers brought from the Alps.

13785.q: Roughly how many years ago did the last Ice Age end?
13785.e: About 10,000 to 12,000 years ago, the climate became much warmer. The glaciers retreated into the Alps.
13785.m: The last Ice Age ended about 10,000 years ago.

13786.q: When were the glaciers in Switzerland at their largest during the last Ice Age?
13786.e: About 24,000 years ago, the glaciers covered large parts of the Swiss Plateau. In the Alps, only the highest peaks stuck out of the ice.
13786.m: About 24,000 years ago, Switzerland was most heavily covered by glaciers.

13787.q: How far did the Rhône Glacier reach during the last Ice Age?
a: As far as the area around Solothurn
13787.e: The Rhône Glacier flowed from Valais over Lake Geneva onto the Swiss Plateau. It reached as far as the area around Solothurn.
13787.m: The Ice Age Rhône Glacier reached as far as the area around Solothurn.

a: A ridge of rock debris left by a glacier
13788.e: Glaciers push stones, gravel and sand in front of them and carry them along their sides. These deposits form ridges called moraines.
13788.m: Moraines are ridges of debris left by glaciers.

13789.q: Which two animals are typical of the last Ice Age?
13789.e: The mammoth and woolly rhinoceros had thick fur against the cold. Both are extinct today.
13789.m: The mammoth and woolly rhinoceros lived in the Ice Age and are extinct today.

13790.q: What happened to the sea level during the Ice Age?
a: It was much lower than today
It was much higher than today
It was the same as today
It changed a lot every day
13790.e: A lot of water was locked up in the huge masses of ice. That is why the sea level was about 120 metres lower and land bridges appeared.
13790.m: In the Ice Age, the sea level was much lower than today.

13791.q: How did many lakes on the Swiss Plateau form?
13791.e: The Ice Age glaciers carved out deep basins. After the ice melted, they filled with water, as with Lake Zurich.
13791.m: Many Swiss lakes lie in basins scoured out by glaciers.

13792.q: Which tool is seen as the typical all-purpose tool of the Old Stone Age?
a: The stone axe with a hole
13792.e: It could probably be used for cutting, scraping, chopping and digging. Hand axes were made for more than a million years.
13792.m: The hand axe was the all-purpose tool of the Old Stone Age.

13793.q: Roughly how old are the oldest known hand axes?
13793.e: The oldest hand axes come from Africa. They were probably made by Homo erectus.
13793.m: The oldest hand axes are more than a million years old.

13794.q: Why was flint a popular material for tools?
13794.e: If you strike flint skilfully, thin pieces with very sharp edges split off. Blades, scrapers and points were made from them.
13794.m: Flint gives very sharp edges when struck.

13795.q: What was a Stone Age scraper used for?
13795.e: The scraper was used to remove fat and bits of meat from the inside of skins. Then clothes and tents could be made from them.
13795.m: People worked animal skins with scrapers.

13796.q: What did people at the end of the Old Stone Age need bone sewing needles for?
13796.e: Needles with an eye made it possible to sew skins together neatly. Well-fitting clothes helped against the cold of the Ice Age.
13796.m: Bone needles made sewn fur clothing possible.

13797.e: Microliths are typical of the Middle Stone Age. They were used, for example, as tips and barbs in arrows.
13797.m: Microliths are tiny stone blades from the Middle Stone Age.

13798.q: Which glue were even the Neanderthals able to make?
13798.e: Birch tar is made by heating birch bark without air. It was used to glue stone points to wooden shafts; the oldest finds are more than 200,000 years old.
13798.m: Birch tar was a Stone Age glue.

13799.q: What was the polished stone axe of the New Stone Age mainly used for?
13799.e: The farmers needed wood for houses and space for fields. With the polished stone axe they could cut down trees.
13799.m: Farmers cleared forest with polished stone axes.

a: A metal made of copper and tin
13800.e: Obsidian forms when lava cools very quickly. It breaks with extremely sharp edges and was traded over long distances.
13800.m: Obsidian is volcanic glass with very sharp edges.

13801.q: According to current knowledge, which human species was probably the first to use fire?
13801.e: The oldest signs of fire use date from the time of Homo erectus, although some are disputed. Homo erectus lived long before modern humans.

13802.q: In which cave were very old traces of fire use found?
13802.e: In Wonderwerk Cave, burnt bones and plant ash were found. They are about a million years old.
13802.m: Wonderwerk Cave shows traces of fire from about a million years ago.

13803.q: According to current knowledge, since when have people used fire often and regularly?
13803.e: Older traces of fire are rare and partly disputed. From about 400,000 years ago, regularly used fireplaces are found at many sites.
13803.m: People have used fire regularly for about 400,000 years.

13804.q: Why was cooking food a big advantage?
a: Cooked food is easier to digest
Cooked food does not need chewing
13804.e: Heating makes meat and plants softer and easier to digest. It also kills some germs.
13804.m: Cooked food is easier to digest than raw food.

13805.q: Which two materials were struck together to make sparks?
13805.e: If you strike flint against pyrite, hot sparks are produced. These fall onto easily burning tinder.
13805.m: You can strike sparks with flint and pyrite.

a: A tree fungus that smoulders easily
A type of grass for weaving
13806.e: Tinder fungus grows on trees. When dried, a single spark makes it start to smoulder.
13806.m: Tinder fungus is a tree fungus that can be used to start a fire.

13807.q: How does a fire drill work?
a: Through the friction heat of a spinning wooden stick
Through sunlight in a drop of water
By banging two pieces of wood together
13807.e: A wooden stick is spun quickly on a board. The friction makes an ember, which is fanned into a fire with tinder.
13807.m: With a fire drill, friction makes enough heat for an ember.

13808.q: What did Ötzi probably carry embers in?
a: In a container made of birch bark
13808.e: Pieces of charcoal were found in one of Ötzi's birch bark containers. He could carry embers in it; he also had tinder fungus with him.
13808.m: Ötzi probably carried embers in a birch bark container.

13809.q: What protection did fire give at night?
a: It kept insects away for ever
13809.e: Many predators avoid fire. It also gave light and warmth, and the group sat together around the fire.
13809.m: Fire gave warmth and light and protected against wild animals.

13810.q: In which year was Lascaux Cave discovered?
13810.e: Four teenagers discovered the cave in September 1940 in the Dordogne in France.
13810.m: Lascaux Cave was discovered by teenagers in 1940.

13812.q: How did many experts first react to the discovery of the paintings at Altamira?
a: They immediately declared them a wonder of the world
They had the cave walled up
They wanted to paint over the pictures
13812.e: People did not believe Stone Age humans could make such art. Only when similar paintings became known in France from 1901 were they accepted as genuine.
13812.m: The paintings at Altamira were at first thought to be fakes.

13813.q: Which animals are shown unusually often in Chauvet Cave?
13813.e: Chauvet Cave in France, discovered in 1994, shows many dangerous animals that are rare in other caves. Its oldest pictures are more than 30,000 years old.
13813.m: Many lions and rhinos are painted in Chauvet Cave.

13814.q: What did Old Stone Age people use to paint red and yellow colours?
13814.e: Ochre is an earth that contains iron. Black was made from charcoal or manganese ore.
13814.m: Red and yellow cave paints were made from ochre.

13815.q: What is shown most often in Old Stone Age cave pictures?
13815.e: Mainly horses, bison, deer and aurochs were painted. People appear only rarely.

13816.q: What do we know today about the purpose of cave paintings?
a: It has not been clearly explained
They were proven to be calendars
They were proven to decorate living spaces
13816.e: There are various ideas, for example rituals or hunting magic. Researchers do not have a definite answer.
13816.m: Why the cave pictures were painted is still not known for sure.

13817.q: What did the artists use to light up the dark caves?
a: Lamps made of stone and animal fat
13817.e: Hollowed-out stones in which animal fat burned with a wick have been found in caves. Torches were also used.
13817.m: People painted in the caves by the light of fat lamps and torches.

13818.q: What is the change from hunting and gathering to farming and keeping animals called?
13818.e: Farming changed people's lives completely. That is why it is called a revolution, even though it took thousands of years.
13818.m: The Neolithic Revolution is the change to a farming way of life.

13819.q: Which types of grain did the first farmers grow?
13819.e: Emmer and einkorn are early types of wheat. Together with barley they are among the oldest cultivated grains.
13819.m: Emmer, einkorn and barley are among the oldest grains.

13820.q: Which pulses did the first farmers in the Near East grow?
13820.e: Like the early grains, peas and lentils come from the Near East. They provided important protein.
13820.m: Peas and lentils are among the oldest crops.

13821.q: What did New Stone Age farmers use flax for?
13821.e: Threads and linen cloth were woven from the fibres of flax. Oil could be made from the seeds.
13821.m: Farmers made linen cloth from flax.

13822.q: How did New Stone Age farmers make flour from grain?
13822.e: The grains were ground on a flat stone slab with a rubbing stone. It was hard and slow work.
13822.m: In the New Stone Age, grain was ground with grinding stones.

13823.e: Farmers cut down trees and burned the forest. At the same time, the ash fertilised the soil.
13823.m: In slash-and-burn, forest is burned to make fields.

13824.q: What did the first farmers use to harvest their grain?
13824.e: Sharp flint blades were set into handles of wood or antler. They were used to cut off the ears of grain.
13824.m: The first farmers harvested with flint sickles.

13825.q: Which plant did New Stone Age farmers in Europe not know yet?
13825.e: The potato comes from South America. It only reached Europe in the 16th century.
13825.m: The potato came to Europe from America much later.

13826.q: What did New Stone Age farmers store their supplies in?
13826.e: With farming, pottery became important. Grain and other supplies could be stored and cooked in clay pots.
13826.m: Farmers stored their supplies in clay pots.

13827.q: What is it called when people turn wild animals into domestic animals over many generations?
13827.e: In domestication, people choose animals with useful features over a long time. This is how domestic animals come about.
13827.m: Wild animals become domestic animals through domestication.

13828.q: Which animal was the first to be domesticated, already by hunter-gatherers?
13828.e: The dog is descended from the wolf. It lived with people long before the first farmers.
13828.m: The dog is humans' oldest domestic animal.

13829.q: Which animals were among the first farm animals in the Near East?
13829.e: Goats and sheep were tamed in the Near East about 10,000 years ago or even earlier. They provided meat, milk and skins.
13829.m: Goats and sheep are among the oldest farm animals.

13830.q: Which wild animal are domestic cattle descended from?
13830.e: The aurochs was a large wild ox. It was bred into domestic cattle in the Near East.
13830.m: Domestic cattle are descended from the aurochs.

13831.q: Are there still wild aurochs today?
13831.e: The last aurochs died in 1627 in Poland. Today only cattle descended from it remain.

13832.q: Which wild animal is the domestic pig descended from?
13832.e: Wild boar were tamed in the New Stone Age. Pigs mainly provided meat.
13832.m: The domestic pig is descended from the wild boar.

13833.q: What advantage did keeping livestock have over hunting?
a: No more animal feed was needed
People no longer had to work
13833.e: The animals were a kind of living food store. People no longer had to rely on luck when hunting.
13833.m: Keeping livestock made the supply of meat more reliable.

13834.q: Which of these animals did New Stone Age farmers in Central Europe not keep yet?
13834.e: Chickens come from Asia. They only reached Central Europe long after the New Stone Age.
13834.m: Chickens were only kept in Central Europe after the New Stone Age.

13835.q: What else did farmers use cattle for towards the end of the New Stone Age?
13835.e: Cattle are strong and have great stamina. They pulled simple ards and later also carts.
13835.m: Cattle were also used to pull ploughs and carts.

13836.e: Settled people live in the same place all year round. Farming made this necessary.
13836.m: Settled people live permanently in a fixed place.

13837.q: Why did the first farmers have to settle down?
a: They had to stay near their fields
They had no shoes any more
13837.e: It takes months from sowing to harvest. The fields had to be looked after and protected from animals.
13837.m: If you farm fields, you have to stay near them.

13838.q: What is typical of the houses of the first farmers in Central Europe?
a: Long houses made of wood and clay
Round houses made of stone blocks
13838.e: The farmers of the Linear Pottery culture built longhouses of wooden posts. The walls were made of wattle and daub.
13838.m: The first farmers in Central Europe lived in longhouses of wood and clay.

13839.q: In which present-day country is the early large settlement of Çatalhöyük?
13839.e: About 9000 years ago, Çatalhöyük in Anatolia was one of the largest settlements in the world. The mud-brick houses stood close together.
13839.m: Çatalhöyük in Turkey is one of the oldest large settlements.

13840.q: How did the people of Çatalhöyük usually enter their houses?
a: Through an opening in the roof
Through a door in the cellar
Through a gate in the town wall
13840.e: The houses stood so close together that there were hardly any streets. People walked over the roofs and climbed down into the house on ladders.
13840.m: In Çatalhöyük, people entered houses through the roof.

13841.q: What effect did settling down have on the population?
a: The population stayed exactly the same
13841.e: Farming fed more people on the same area of land than hunting. That is why the population grew.
13841.m: The population grew when people settled down.

13842.q: What new problem came from living close together with domestic animals?
13842.e: Many germs passed from animals to humans. In crowded settlements they spread more quickly.
13842.m: Living with animals encouraged infectious diseases.

13843.q: What became more important than before when people settled down?
a: Luck in hunting and reading tracks
13843.e: If you live in one place, you can own supplies, tools and houses. This also led to differences between rich and poor.
13843.m: When people settled down, possessions and supplies became more important.

13844.q: Which ancient town in the West Bank is considered one of the oldest settlements in the world?
13844.e: Jericho was already settled more than 10,000 years ago. A stone tower from the New Stone Age is well known.
13844.m: Jericho is one of the oldest settlements in the world.

13845.q: Since which year have the “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps” been UNESCO World Heritage?
13845.e: UNESCO added the sites to the World Heritage List in 2011. Six countries nominated them together.
13845.m: The pile dwellings around the Alps have been UNESCO World Heritage since 2011.

13846.q: In which country are just over half of the UNESCO World Heritage pile dwelling sites?
13846.e: 56 of the 111 sites are in Switzerland. The rest are in Italy, Germany, France, Austria and Slovenia.
13846.m: Just over half of the World Heritage pile dwelling sites are in Switzerland.

13847.q: From what period do the World Heritage pile dwelling settlements date?
13847.e: The settlements date from the New Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the early Iron Age.
13847.m: Pile dwellings existed from about 5000 to 500 BC.

13848.q: Why did remains of pile dwellings appear at Lake Zurich in the winter of 1853/54?
a: The water level was very low
An earthquake raised the lake bed
The lake had dried up completely
13848.e: Near Meilen, the lake bed was exposed because of dry weather. Hundreds of posts and finds sparked research into pile dwellings.
13848.m: Research into pile dwellings began in 1854 when the water of Lake Zurich was low.

13849.q: Who made the pile dwellings known through his reports from 1854 onwards?
13849.e: The Zurich antiquarian Ferdinand Keller interpreted the finds from Lake Zurich as the remains of settlements. He created the idea of villages on platforms above the water.
13849.m: Ferdinand Keller is seen as the founder of pile dwelling research.

13850.q: Why have so many things made of wood and plants survived in pile dwelling settlements?
a: Under water there is no oxygen for rotting
The lake water is especially salty
The things were copies made of stone
13850.e: There is no oxygen in wet ground and under water. That is why wood, seeds, cloth and even food remains hardly decay.
13850.m: Wood and plants survive in damp ground without oxygen.

13851.q: How can the year in which the posts were felled often be found exactly?
13851.e: In dendrochronology, the tree rings of the wood are compared with a tree-ring chart. This shows exactly the year the tree was felled.
13851.m: Dendrochronology dates wood by its tree rings.

13852.q: Which important finds from the late New Stone Age are known from pile dwellings?
13852.e: The wooden wheels from pile dwelling settlements are about 5000 years old. They are among the oldest wheels in the world.
13852.m: Some of the oldest wheels in the world were found in pile dwellings.

13853.q: What do researchers say today about where many pile dwelling houses stood?
a: Many stood on the shore, not over open water
All stood in the middle of the lake
13853.e: People used to imagine villages on platforms in the lake. Today we know that many houses stood on lake shores and in moors, often with raised floors.
13853.m: Many pile dwelling houses stood on the shore and not in the middle of the lake.

13854.q: What are New Stone Age cultures such as the Cortaillod culture usually named after?
a: An important site where finds were made
13854.e: Because we do not know the names of the peoples, cultures are named after sites. The Cortaillod culture is named after a village on Lake Neuchâtel.
13854.m: Prehistoric cultures are often named after sites.

13855.q: Roughly when was the Bronze Age in Central Europe and the area of present-day Switzerland?
13855.e: In Central Europe, people began to make bronze around 2200 BC. Around 800 BC, iron slowly took over.
13855.m: In our region, the Bronze Age lasted from about 2200 to 800 BC.

13857.q: What are the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age named after?
a: The most important material for tools
The places of the first finds
13857.e: In 1836, the Danish scholar Christian Jürgensen Thomsen sorted finds by the material of the tools. This created the three-age system.
13857.m: The periods of prehistory are named after the material of their tools.

13858.q: In which order do the three great periods of prehistory follow each other?
a: Stone Age, Bronze Age, Iron Age
Bronze Age, Stone Age, Iron Age
Iron Age, Bronze Age, Stone Age
Stone Age, Iron Age, Bronze Age
13858.e: First people used tools made of stone, then of bronze and finally of iron. Iron is harder to obtain and therefore came last.
13858.m: The Stone Age is followed by the Bronze Age and then the Iron Age.

13859.q: In which present-day country was the Nebra Sky Disc found in 1999?
13859.e: Illegal treasure hunters found the disc in 1999 with a metal detector on the Mittelberg near Nebra in Saxony-Anhalt. Today it is in the State Museum in Halle.
13859.m: The Nebra Sky Disc comes from Saxony-Anhalt in Germany.

13860.q: What is shown on the Nebra Sky Disc?
a: The sun or full moon, a crescent moon and stars
A warrior with sword and shield
The family tree of a noble family
13860.e: Golden heavenly bodies are set into the bronze disc. It is considered one of the oldest realistic pictures of the sky in the world.
13860.m: The Nebra Sky Disc shows the sun, moon and stars.

13861.q: According to current knowledge, around what time was the Nebra Sky Disc buried?
13861.e: The objects found with it, such as swords and axes, point to the early Bronze Age around 1600 BC. The disc itself is probably a little older.
13861.m: The Nebra Sky Disc was buried around 1600 BC.

13862.q: Which famous gold find came to light in Zurich in 1906 during work on the railway line?
13862.e: A worker found the gold bowl in Zurich-Altstetten in 1906. It is decorated with suns and moons and today belongs to the Swiss National Museum.
13862.m: The Altstetten gold bowl was found in Zurich in 1906.

13863.q: What have the pile dwellings around the Alps belonged to since 2011?
13863.e: In 2011, UNESCO listed a total of 111 pile dwelling sites in six countries. Many date from the New Stone Age and the Bronze Age.
13863.m: The pile dwellings around the Alps are UNESCO World Heritage.

13864.q: In which country are most of the UNESCO World Heritage pile dwelling sites?
13864.e: Of the 111 sites, 56 are in Switzerland, more than half. Italy and Germany come next.
13864.m: More than half of the World Heritage pile dwellings are in Switzerland.

13865.q: Why are wood and plant remains from pile dwelling settlements often so well preserved?
a: They lay in wet ground without air
They lay in hot desert sand
13865.e: In damp ground on the lake shore or in a moor, hardly any oxygen reaches the wood. That is why bacteria and fungi can hardly break it down.
13865.m: Wet ground without air protects wood from rotting.

13866.q: Where does the Tumulus culture of the Middle Bronze Age get its name from?
a: The dead were buried under mounds of earth
The graves were in rock caves
The dead were sunk in lakes
13866.e: At this time, mounds of earth and stones were piled up over the graves of important people. Many of these burial mounds can still be seen today.
13866.m: In the Tumulus culture, the dead were buried under burial mounds.

13867.q: How were the dead usually buried in the Urnfield culture of the late Bronze Age?
a: They were cremated and the ashes buried in urns
They were embalmed and placed in pyramids
They were sent out to sea in boats
They were laid unburnt in stone boxes
13867.e: The ashes were put into clay pots called urns. Many urns were buried next to each other in fields, hence the name Urnfield.
13867.m: The Urnfield culture is named after its cemeteries with urns.

13868.q: What do archaeologists mean by a hoard?
a: Objects that were buried or hidden on purpose
13868.e: In the Bronze Age, axes, jewellery or weapons were often buried together. They may have been offerings to gods or hidden valuables.
13868.m: A hoard is treasure that was deliberately put down.

13869.q: Why did tin often have to be traded from far away in the Bronze Age?
a: It was found in only a few places
It was too heavy to carry
13869.e: Tin for bronze was only found in a few places, for example in Cornwall in England. That is why long trade networks developed in the Bronze Age.
13869.m: Bronze needed tin, which was often traded from far away.

13871.q: Which sought-after trade good from the Baltic Sea reached the Mediterranean in the Bronze Age?
13871.e: Amber is fossilised tree resin and was made into jewellery. It was carried south along long trade routes.
13871.m: Amber from the Baltic was a valuable trade good in the Bronze Age.

13872.q: How did bronze change society in the Bronze Age?
a: Bigger differences between rich and poor developed
13872.e: Those who controlled raw materials, trade and metalworking became powerful. Rich graves show that an upper class formed.
13872.m: A rich upper class formed in the Bronze Age.

13873.q: Where was bronze made much earlier than in Central Europe?
a: In the Near East and in Egypt
13873.e: In the Near East, bronze was already being made around 3300 BC, and in Egypt from about 2700 BC. The knowledge only spread to Central Europe later.
13873.m: The Bronze Age began earlier in the Near East than in our region.

13874.q: Where were the Bronze Age pile dwelling settlements in Switzerland usually located?
a: On lake shores and in moors
13874.e: Many villages stood on the shores of lakes such as Lake Zurich or Lake Neuchâtel. The houses stood on posts or on the damp ground of the shore.
13874.m: Pile dwellings stood by lakes and in moors.

13875.q: What does the huge Greek bronze vessel in the grave of the Celtic Lady of Vix show?
a: Celtic nobles had contacts as far as Greece
The Celts did not know about metal
13875.e: The Vix krater is 1.64 metres tall and weighs more than 200 kilograms. Such a splendid piece came north over long routes as a gift or trade good.
13875.m: The Vix krater shows contacts between the Celts and the Greeks.

13876.q: What is the earlier Iron Age in Central Europe called?
13876.e: The Hallstatt period lasted from about 800 to 450 BC. It is named after a famous cemetery.
13876.m: The earlier Iron Age is called the Hallstatt period.

13877.q: In which country is Hallstatt, the place the earlier Iron Age is named after?
13877.e: Hallstatt is in the Salzkammergut in Upper Austria. A large Iron Age cemetery was discovered there.
13877.m: Hallstatt is in the Salzkammergut in Austria.

13878.q: How did the people of Hallstatt become rich in the Iron Age?
13878.e: Salt was already mined in the salt mountain at Hallstatt in prehistoric times. Salt was very valuable because it could be used to preserve meat.
13878.m: Hallstatt became rich through salt mining.

13879.q: What was found in the cemetery at Hallstatt?
a: Many graves with grave goods such as jewellery and weapons
13879.e: From 1846 onwards, more than a thousand graves were uncovered at Hallstatt. The rich grave goods show how wealthy the people had become through salt mining.
13879.m: More than a thousand rich graves were found at Hallstatt.

13880.q: What is the later Iron Age, which began around 450 BC, called?
13880.e: The La Tène period lasted from about 450 BC until the end of the 1st century BC. At this time the Celts, including the Helvetii, lived in our region.
13880.m: The later Iron Age is called the La Tène period.

13881.q: On which lake is the site of La Tène, after which the later Iron Age is named?
13881.e: La Tène is on the northern shore of Lake Neuchâtel in the canton of Neuchâtel. The whole period is named after this Swiss site.
13881.m: La Tène is on Lake Neuchâtel in Switzerland.

13882.q: Why were many finds suddenly made at La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel?
a: The water level of the lake was low
A fisherman caught them in his net
13882.e: In 1857 the lake level was low. Many iron swords and other objects appeared in the shallow water.
13882.m: When the water was low, many finds appeared at La Tène.

13883.q: What kind of finds turned up especially often at La Tène?
a: Weapons such as swords, lances and shields
13883.e: Many swords, spearheads, shields and tools were found. There were also jewellery, coins and skeletons.
13883.m: Many Celtic weapons were found at La Tène.

13884.q: What brought the Iron Age to an end in the area of present-day Switzerland?
a: The founding of the Swiss Confederation
The end of the last Ice Age
13884.e: At the end of the 1st century BC, the area came under Roman rule. After that we speak of the Roman period.
13884.m: In our region, the Iron Age ended with the Romans.

13885.q: Where did the Iron Age begin much earlier than in Central Europe?
13885.e: In the Middle East, the Iron Age began as early as around 1200 BC. In our region it only started around 800 BC.
13885.m: The Iron Age began much earlier in the Middle East than in our region.

13886.q: How can we tell that a powerful Celtic chieftain lay in the grave at Hochdorf?
a: From the rich grave goods such as a wagon, gold and bronze vessels
From an inscription with his name
From a painting on the grave wall
13886.e: The chieftain of Hochdorf lay on a splendid bronze couch. A wagon, gold jewellery and large drinking vessels were also found in the grave.
13886.m: Rich grave goods show that a chieftain was buried at Hochdorf.

13887.q: What do Greek goods found at the Heuneburg on the Danube show?
a: That there was trade with the Greeks
That the Celts lived in Greece
That the Romans built a town there
13887.e: The Heuneburg was a Celtic chieftain's seat of the Hallstatt period. Greek pottery shows that goods came north along long trade routes.
13887.m: The Heuneburg had trade contacts reaching as far as the Greeks.

13888.q: What does the famous stone statue from the Glauberg in Hesse show?
a: A Celtic warrior with sword and shield
13888.e: The roughly life-size figure was found in 1996. It carries a sword, a shield and a neck ring, and wears a crown that looks like two leaves.
13888.m: The statue of a Celtic chieftain was found at the Glauberg.

13889.q: On which hill overlooking Zurich was there an important Celtic settlement in the Iron Age?
13889.e: On the Uetliberg there was a chieftain's seat in the Hallstatt period and later a Celtic oppidum. There are burial mounds nearby.
13889.m: People already lived on the Uetliberg in the Iron Age.

13890.q: In which canton was the Celtic gold treasure of Erstfeld found in 1962?
13890.e: Construction workers found the treasure between boulders under several metres of scree. Erstfeld is on the route to the Gotthard.
13890.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure comes from the canton of Uri.

13891.q: What does the Celtic gold treasure of Erstfeld consist of?
13891.e: The treasure consists of seven rings made of very pure gold. Together they weigh about 640 grams.
13891.m: The Erstfeld treasure consists of gold rings.

13892.q: Roughly when does the Erstfeld gold treasure date from?
13892.e: The rings are usually dated to around 300 BC. That is the La Tène period, the later Iron Age.
13892.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure is about 2300 years old.

13893.q: How is the Erstfeld gold treasure most often explained?
a: As an offering for a safe crossing of the Alps
As the dowry of a princess from Egypt
As the treasure of a medieval monastery
13893.e: The treasure lay on an important Alpine route. Many experts think it was a gift to a god, but this is not certain.
13893.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure was probably an offering.

13894.q: Which well-known Celtic cemetery of the La Tène period is in the canton of Bern?
13894.e: More than 200 graves were found at Münsingen. Because the graves were laid out one after another, they show the development of the La Tène period very clearly.
13894.m: The cemetery at Münsingen is an important La Tène site.

13895.q: Roughly how much tin does typical bronze contain?
13895.e: Bronze usually consists of about 90 parts copper and 10 parts tin. The exact share varied depending on the workshop and purpose.
13895.m: Bronze is mostly copper with a small amount of tin.

13896.q: What advantage does bronze have over pure copper?
13896.e: The tin makes the metal much harder. Tools and weapons made of bronze stayed sharp for longer.
13896.m: Bronze is harder than pure copper.

13897.q: At roughly what temperature does copper melt?
13897.e: Melting copper needed a very hot fire. With charcoal and bellows, such temperatures could be reached.
13897.m: Copper melts at about 1085 degrees Celsius.

13898.q: At roughly what temperature does tin melt?
13898.e: Tin has a much lower melting point than copper. That is why it is easy to stir into molten copper.
13898.m: Tin melts at only about 232 degrees Celsius.

13899.q: How were bronze axes usually made in the Bronze Age?
a: Liquid bronze was poured into moulds
They were carved from blocks of bronze
They were ground out of bronze rocks
13899.e: The bronze was melted and poured into moulds of stone or clay. Then the piece was hammered and ground.
13899.m: Bronze objects were cast in moulds.

13900.q: In lost-wax casting, what is the model that is later melted out made of?
13900.e: A model is shaped from wax and covered with clay. When heated, the wax flows out and bronze is poured into the hollow space.
13900.m: In lost-wax casting, a wax model is replaced by bronze.

13901.q: In what kind of furnace was iron obtained from ore in the Iron Age?
13901.e: The bloomery was a small shaft furnace made of clay. Blast furnaces only appeared in Europe much later.
13901.m: In the Iron Age, iron was obtained in a bloomery.

13902.q: Which fuel was used in a bloomery?
13902.e: Charcoal and crushed ore were layered in the furnace in turns. The charcoal provided heat and helped to free the iron from the ore.

13903.q: What did the iron that came out of a bloomery look like?
13903.e: In a bloomery, the iron did not become completely liquid. It formed a spongy lump called a bloom, which still had to be forged.
13903.m: A lump of iron with slag came out of the bloomery.

13904.q: Roughly what temperatures were reached in a bloomery?
13904.e: The temperature was high enough to turn the ore into iron. But the iron did not melt completely.
13904.m: A bloomery got hotter than 1000 degrees.

13905.q: Why did the iron in a bloomery not become completely liquid?
a: The iron was cooled with water beforehand
13905.e: The melting point of iron is higher than the temperature in a bloomery. This was actually wanted, because liquid cast iron is brittle and cannot be forged.
13905.m: Iron has a higher melting point than copper.

13907.q: What had to be done with the bloom before tools could be made from it?
a: It was heated and forged again and again
13907.e: Hammering squeezed slag and bits of charcoal out of the iron. Only then did you have usable wrought iron.
13907.m: The bloom was forged to remove the slag.

13908.q: Why did iron gradually replace bronze?
a: Iron ore is much more common than copper and tin
Iron shines more beautifully than bronze
13908.e: Bronze needed tin, which was rare and had to be traded over long distances. Iron ore, on the other hand, was found in many areas, including the Jura.
13908.m: Iron ore could be found almost everywhere, but tin could not.

13909.q: Which ore was already mined in the Jura in ancient times?
13909.e: In the Jura there is iron ore in the form of small grains, called pea ore. Iron was obtained from it even in ancient times.
13909.m: In the Jura, iron was obtained from pea ore.

13910.q: What do old heaps of slag in the Oberhalbstein in the Grisons prove?
a: Copper was produced there in prehistoric times
There was once a volcano there
There was a Roman camp there
13910.e: Slag is waste produced when ore is smelted. A lot of copper was produced in the Oberhalbstein around 1000 BC.
13910.m: Copper was also produced in Switzerland in prehistoric times.

13911.q: What metal was the axe of the glacier mummy Ötzi made of?
13911.e: Ötzi lived around 3300 BC, before the Bronze Age. At that time people already knew pure copper, but not yet bronze.
13911.m: Ötzi's axe was made of copper.

13912.q: What are bellows used for in metalworking?
a: They blow air into the fire to make it hotter
They cool the metal after forging
They grind the ore into powder
13912.e: With more oxygen, charcoal burns hotter. This is the only way to reach the high temperatures needed to obtain metal.

13913.e: In smelting, heat frees the metal from the rock. Rock that contains metal is called ore.
13913.m: In smelting, metal is obtained from ore.

13914.q: What is the alloy of copper and zinc, which should not be confused with bronze, called?
13914.e: Brass looks similar to bronze but contains zinc. Brass was only made in larger amounts in Roman times.
13914.m: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

13915.q: What did Greek writers call the peoples north of the Alps?
13915.e: Greek authors of the 6th and 5th centuries BC spoke of the Keltoi. Our word Celts comes from this.
13915.m: The word Celts comes from the Greek Keltoi.

13916.q: What did the Romans call the Celts in the area of present-day France?
13916.e: The Romans called the country Gaul and the people Gauls. Caesar conquered Gaul in the Gallic War.
13916.m: The Romans called the Celts in France Gauls.

13917.q: What were the tasks of the druids among the Celts?
a: They were priests, judges and teachers
13917.e: The druids belonged to the educated upper class. They led sacrifices, judged disputes and passed on their knowledge.
13917.m: Druids were the priests, judges and teachers of the Celts.

13918.q: According to Caesar, how long could a druid's training last?
13918.e: Caesar reports that some students studied for up to 20 years. They had to learn many verses by heart.
13918.m: A druid's training could last up to 20 years.

13919.q: According to Caesar, which duties were druids exempt from?
13919.e: These privileges made the druids highly respected. That is why many young men wanted to become druids.
13919.m: Druids did not have to do military service or pay taxes.

13920.q: How did the Celts mainly pass on religious knowledge?
13920.e: Religious teachings were apparently deliberately not written down. For other things, however, the Celts did use writing, for example Greek or Latin letters.
13920.m: The Celts passed on their religious knowledge by word of mouth.

13921.q: Which city did a Celtic army under Brennus conquer around 387 BC?
13921.e: The Celts defeated the Romans and occupied most of Rome. The Romans long remembered this event as a heavy defeat.
13921.m: Around 387 BC, Celts under Brennus conquered Rome.

13922.q: Where did the Celts live at the height of their power?
13922.e: Celtic tribes lived from Spain to Britain and as far as Asia Minor. Some of them lived in the area of present-day Switzerland.
13922.m: The Celts lived in large parts of Europe.

13923.q: Which of these languages is a Celtic language still spoken today?
13923.e: Welsh, Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Breton are still spoken today. Romansh, on the other hand, is a Romance language.

13924.e: Oppida existed mainly in the 2nd and 1st centuries BC, often on important trade routes. They were protected by ramparts or walls and had workshops and markets.
13924.m: An oppidum was a fortified Celtic town.

13925.q: Where did the Celts get the model for their first coins?
a: They took them over from China
They invented them without a model
13925.e: Celtic mercenaries came to know Greek gold coins. Later the Celts minted their own coins based on them.
13925.m: The first Celtic coins copied Greek ones.

13926.q: What did the Celts base their calendar on?
13926.e: A Celtic calendar from France shows months based on the moon. They were adjusted to fit the solar year.
13926.m: The Celts watched the moon and the sun closely.

13928.q: At which town was Vercingetorix besieged and defeated by Caesar in 52 BC?
13928.e: Caesar had Alesia surrounded with ramparts. After the defeat, Gaul was largely under Roman control.

13929.q: What is the work in which Julius Caesar reports on his war against the Gauls called?
13929.e: In Latin the work is called “De bello Gallico”. In it Caesar also describes the Helvetii, although from his own Roman point of view.

13930.e: Torcs were made of gold, silver or bronze. They often showed high rank or had a religious meaning.
13930.m: A torc is a Celtic neck ring.

13931.q: According to ancient reports, which plant was sacred to the druids?
13931.e: The Roman Pliny reports that druids cut mistletoe from oak trees with a golden sickle. Mistletoe was thought to cure many illnesses.
13931.m: Mistletoe was sacred to the druids.

13932.q: Which decorations are typical of the Celtic art style of the La Tène period?
13932.e: Celtic artists loved wavy tendrils, spirals and interlaced patterns. Plants and animals often merge into each other.
13932.m: Celtic art is full of spirals and tendrils.

13933.q: What does the Celtic place-name ending “-dunum”, as in Eburodunum for Yverdon, mean?
13933.e: Many place names go back to Celtic words. “Dunum” meant a fort or fortified settlement.
13933.m: The ending dunum means fortified place.

13934.q: Which animal was so important to the Celts that they worshipped a goddess of its own for it?
13934.e: The goddess Epona protected horses and their riders. Later Roman soldiers worshipped her too.
13934.m: The Celts worshipped a horse goddess.

13935.q: Where did the Helvetii mainly live in the 1st century BC?
a: On the Swiss Plateau between the Jura and the Alps
In the valleys of the Grisons
13935.e: Caesar describes their territory between the Jura, the Rhine, Lake Geneva and the Rhône. This roughly matches today's Swiss Plateau.
13935.m: The Helvetii lived on the Swiss Plateau.

13936.q: Which great people did the Helvetii belong to?
13936.e: The Helvetii were a Celtic tribe. Other Celtic tribes lived in Gaul, Britain and southern Germany.

13937.q: Which language did the Helvetii speak?
13937.e: The Helvetii spoke a Celtic language. German and French only came to Switzerland much later.

13938.q: How did most Helvetii make a living?
a: From farming crops and keeping animals
13938.e: Most Helvetii were farmers. They grew grain and kept cattle, pigs and sheep.

13939.q: Which Roman general defeated the Helvetii in 58 BC?
13939.e: Julius Caesar confronted the Helvetii in Gaul and defeated them. Hannibal was not a Roman but an enemy of Rome.
13939.m: Caesar defeated the Helvetii in 58 BC.

13940.q: Why do we know about the Helvetii mainly from Roman reports?
a: The Helvetii hardly wrote anything down about themselves
The Romans banned the Helvetii from speaking
The Helvetii lived after the Romans
13940.e: The Celts mostly passed on their knowledge by word of mouth. That is why we rely on Romans such as Caesar and on archaeological finds.
13940.m: It is mainly Romans who tell us about the Helvetii.

13941.q: Who left their territory with the Helvetii in 58 BC?
a: Whole families with wagons and livestock
13941.e: The Helvetii wanted to find a new area to settle. That is why men, women and children set off with their belongings.
13941.m: Whole families took part when the Helvetii set off.

13942.q: According to Caesar, in which year did the Helvetii leave their territory?
13942.e: In spring 58 BC they set off with families and wagons. This was the start of Caesar's Gallic War.
13942.m: The Helvetii set off in 58 BC.

13943.q: In which direction did the Helvetii want to emigrate in 58 BC?
13943.e: According to Caesar, they wanted to travel through Gaul to the west, close to the Atlantic. Researchers disagree about their goal.
13943.m: The Helvetii wanted to move west.

13944.q: At which town did the Helvetii first want to cross the Rhône in 58 BC?
13944.e: At Geneva, a bridge led over the Rhône into Roman territory. Caesar had the bridge torn down and the bank fortified.
13944.m: Caesar blocked the Helvetii's way at Geneva.

13945.q: How did the fight between Caesar and the Helvetii end in 58 BC?
13945.e: Caesar defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte in Burgundy. After that they had to return to their territory.
13945.m: Caesar defeated the Helvetii in 58 BC.

13946.q: Why did Caesar send the Helvetii back to their territory after their defeat?
a: So that Germanic tribes would not occupy the empty land
So that they could attack Rome
Because he wanted to look for gold there
Because they wanted to become Romans
13946.e: Caesar did not want Germanic tribes to move into the abandoned land. The Helvetii were to act as a buffer between the Germanic tribes and Roman territory.
13946.m: The Helvetii were meant to protect Rome from the Germanic tribes.

13947.q: What did the Helvetii have to do after their defeat by Caesar?
13947.e: Caesar sent the Helvetii back to the Swiss Plateau. They were to live on the land so that no Germanic tribes moved there.
13947.m: After their defeat, the Helvetii had to return.

13948.q: Why do historians doubt Caesar's numbers about the Helvetii?
a: He probably exaggerated to make his victory seem bigger
There were no numbers back then
13948.e: Caesar also wrote his report to become famous in Rome. A march with hundreds of thousands of people would hardly have been possible.
13948.m: Caesar's numbers about the Helvetii are probably exaggerated.

13949.q: According to Caesar, in which script were the lists he found in the camp of the Helvetii written?
13949.e: Caesar reports tablets with Greek letters. The Celts used this script even though they spoke Celtic.
13949.m: According to Caesar, the Helvetii wrote with Greek letters.

13950.q: According to Caesar, what did the Helvetii do with their villages before leaving?
a: They sold them to the Romans
They gave them to the Germanic tribes
13950.e: According to Caesar, this was to stop anyone from going back. However, archaeologists have found hardly any evidence of such fires.
13950.m: According to Caesar, the Helvetii burned their villages.

13951.q: Why did the Helvetii like to build their fortified settlements on hills or in river bends?
a: They were closer to the gods there
13951.e: Steep slopes or a river all around made things difficult for attackers. The Helvetii also built ramparts and walls.
13951.m: Hills and rivers protected the settlements of the Helvetii.

13952.q: In which present-day Swiss city was there a Helvetian oppidum on the Enge peninsula?
13952.e: The River Aare flows almost all the way round the Enge peninsula in Bern. This natural protection made the place ideal for a fortified settlement.
13952.m: There was a Celtic oppidum on the Enge peninsula in Bern.

13953.q: On which hill in Zurich's old town was there a Celtic settlement?
13953.e: The Lindenhof lies right on the River Limmat. Later the Romans also built a fort there.
13953.m: Celts already lived on the Lindenhof in Zurich.

13954.q: Where does the abbreviation “CH” for Switzerland come from?
13954.e: Confoederatio Helvetica is the Latin name of Switzerland. It recalls the Celtic tribe of the Helvetii.
13954.m: The name Confoederatio Helvetica recalls the Helvetii.

13955.q: What does the Greek name ‘Mesopotamia’ mean?
13955.e: Mesopotamia comes from Greek and means ‘between the rivers’. In German it is therefore also called ‘Zweistromland’, the land of two rivers.
13955.m: Mesopotamia is the land between two rivers.

13956.q: Between which two rivers does Mesopotamia lie?
13956.e: The Euphrates and Tigris brought water and fertile mud to the dry land.
13956.m: The Euphrates and Tigris made Mesopotamia fertile.

13957.q: In which present-day country does most of ancient Mesopotamia lie?
13957.e: The heartland of Mesopotamia is in present-day Iraq, with outer areas in Syria, Turkey and Iran.
13957.m: Most of ancient Mesopotamia lies in present-day Iraq.

13958.q: What is the curved, fertile region from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean, which includes Mesopotamia, called?
13958.e: The ‘Fertile Crescent’ curves like an arc through the Near East. People here began farming and keeping livestock early on.
13958.m: In the Fertile Crescent people began farming early.

13959.q: How did farmers in Mesopotamia get water onto their fields even though there was little rain?
13959.e: People dug canals and ditches to lead river water onto the fields. This needed a lot of shared work and organisation.
13959.m: Canals brought river water to the fields of Mesopotamia.

13960.q: What did people in Mesopotamia mainly build their houses and temples from?
13960.e: Mesopotamia had little stone and wood but plenty of clay. People shaped it into bricks, which were dried in the sun or fired.
13960.m: In Mesopotamia people mainly built with mud bricks.

13961.q: What is a stepped temple tower in Mesopotamia called?
13961.e: A ziggurat is a stepped tower of mud bricks with a shrine at the top. The story of the Tower of Babel probably goes back to the ziggurat of Babylon.
13961.m: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower in Mesopotamia.

13962.q: Which story from Mesopotamia is considered one of the oldest surviving poems in the world?
13962.e: The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of King Gilgamesh of Uruk and his search for immortality. It survived on clay tablets in cuneiform.
13962.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of humanity's oldest poems.

13963.q: Which number system from Mesopotamia do we still use today for telling the time?
13963.e: In Mesopotamia people counted with the base number 60. That is why an hour has 60 minutes and a minute 60 seconds.
13963.m: The 60 minutes of an hour come from Mesopotamia.

13964.e: The Sumerians lived in southern Mesopotamia near the Persian Gulf. They founded some of the first cities there.
13964.m: The Sumerians lived in southern Mesopotamia.

13965.q: Which Sumerian city is considered one of the first big cities in the world?
13965.e: Around 3000 BC, Uruk probably had several tens of thousands of inhabitants. Some of the oldest written records were also found there.
13965.m: Uruk was one of the first big cities in the world.

13966.q: Which important invention used to be credited to the Sumerians, even though finds of similar age also come from Europe?
13966.e: The wheel was known in Mesopotamia more than 5000 years ago. But wheels of similar age were also found in Europe, for example in the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, so it is unclear where it was invented first.
13966.m: Where the wheel was first invented is still unclear.

13967.q: How were the Sumerians organised politically?
13967.e: Each Sumerian city such as Ur, Uruk or Lagash was its own state with its own ruler and its own city god. The cities often quarrelled over water and land.
13967.m: The Sumerians lived in many independent city states.

13968.q: Which famous Sumerian city had a large ziggurat and is named in the Bible as Abraham's place of origin?
13968.e: Ur was an important Sumerian city in the south of present-day Iraq. Its ziggurat has been partly rebuilt.
13968.m: Ur was an important Sumerian city with a large ziggurat.

13969.q: What happened to the Sumerian city states around 2300 BC?
a: A ruler united them into a great empire
They were conquered by the Romans
13969.e: Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities and founded the Akkadian Empire. It is considered one of the first great empires in history.
13969.m: Sargon of Akkad created one of the first great empires.

13970.q: According to Sumerian belief, who was the lord and protector of their city?
13970.e: Every Sumerian city had a protective god. His temple was the most important building and managed a lot of land and supplies.
13970.m: The temple of the city god was the centre of a Sumerian city.

13971.q: Why is the Sumerian language especially difficult for researchers?
a: It is not related to any known language
13971.e: Sumerian is a language isolate, which means it is not related to any other known language. It was worked out mainly thanks to bilingual texts with Akkadian.
13971.m: The language of the Sumerians is not related to any known language.

13972.q: Which Babylonian king had a famous collection of laws written on a stone pillar around 1750 BC?
13972.e: Hammurabi ruled from about 1792 to 1750 BC. His laws survive on a large stele of dark stone.
13972.m: Hammurabi had one of the best-known law codes of ancient times written down.

13973.q: In which museum is the stele with the Code of Hammurabi today?
a: The Swiss National Museum in Zurich
13973.e: French archaeologists found the stele in the winter of 1901/02 in Susa, in present-day Iran. It has been in the Louvre in Paris ever since.
13973.m: Hammurabi's law stele is in the Louvre today.

13974.q: Which principle is typical of many punishments in the Code of Hammurabi?
13974.e: Many punishments matched the harm someone had caused. However, the punishments also depended on whether someone was free, dependent or enslaved.
13974.m: In the Code of Hammurabi the punishment often matched the harm.

13975.q: On which river was the city of Babylon?
13975.e: Babylon lay on the Euphrates, about 90 kilometres south of present-day Baghdad. The river was important for trade and irrigation.
13975.m: Babylon lay on the banks of the Euphrates.

13976.q: Which magnificent blue city gate from Babylon was rebuilt in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin?
13976.e: The Ishtar Gate is decorated with blue glazed bricks and pictures of animals such as lions, bulls and dragons. The Pergamon Museum has been closed since 2023 for a major renovation.
13976.m: The blue Ishtar Gate from Babylon was rebuilt in Berlin.

13977.q: Under which king did Babylon flourish in the 6th century BC?
13977.e: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled from about 605 to 562 BC. He had Babylon magnificently expanded.
13977.m: Under Nebuchadnezzar II Babylon was magnificently expanded.

13978.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is said to have stood in Babylon?
a: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia
13978.e: Ancient writers tell of the Hanging Gardens of Semiramis in Babylon. Archaeologists have still not found certain proof of them.
13978.m: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are a wonder that has never been found for certain.

13979.q: Which people were partly taken away to Babylon after the conquest of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC?
13979.e: Babylonian troops destroyed Jerusalem and took mainly members of the upper class to Babylon. This period is called the Babylonian Exile.
13979.m: In the Babylonian Exile many Jews lived in Babylon, far from their homeland.

13980.q: Which Persian king conquered Babylon in 539 BC?
13980.e: Cyrus II took Babylon in 539 BC. Babylonia thus became part of the Persian Empire.
13980.m: In 539 BC Babylon fell to the Persians.

13981.q: What were the Babylonians especially known for in science?
13981.e: Babylonian scholars observed stars and planets for centuries and recorded the data on clay tablets. They could, for example, predict lunar eclipses.
13981.m: The Babylonians were excellent star watchers and mathematicians.

13982.q: According to what we know today, where was one of the world's first writing systems developed, around 3300 BC?
13982.e: In southern Mesopotamia, clay tablets with written signs from around 3300 BC have been found. Hieroglyphs developed in Egypt at almost the same time.
13982.m: The first writing systems developed in Mesopotamia and Egypt.

13983.q: What did people in Mesopotamia mainly use the first written signs for?
13983.e: The oldest texts are lists of grain, livestock and taxes. Temples and palaces wanted to keep track of their supplies this way.
13983.m: Writing first developed to record supplies and taxes.

13984.q: What do you call a written sign that shows an object as a simplified picture?
13984.e: The first written signs were often pictures, such as a head for ‘head’ or an ear of grain for ‘grain’. Picture signs like these are called pictograms.
13984.m: A pictogram is a written sign in the form of a simple picture.

13985.q: What did the invention of writing mean for the study of history?
a: It ended the Stone Age at once
It only became important in the Middle Ages
13985.e: Times without written sources are called prehistory. History in the proper sense begins with the first texts.
13985.m: History in the narrower sense begins with the invention of writing.

13986.q: Who could usually read and write in the early civilisations?
13986.e: Writing had to be learned for many years in scribal schools. That is why only a few people could write, and scribes were respected.
13986.m: In the early civilisations scribes were a small, respected group.

13987.q: Besides writing, which feature typically belongs to an advanced civilisation?
a: Cities with administration and division of labour
Life as hunters without a fixed home
13987.e: Advanced civilisations had cities, an administration, specialised jobs, religion with temples and writing. Their basis was productive farming.
13987.m: An advanced civilisation has cities, administration, division of labour and writing.

13988.q: In which regions did writing develop independently?
13988.e: Researchers believe that writing was invented several times independently. This is considered certain for Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probable for Egypt.
13988.m: Writing was invented independently in several places in the world.

13989.q: Who lived in what is now Switzerland at the time of the first Egyptian pyramids?
a: Farmers in pile-dwelling villages on lakes
13989.e: In the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, people lived in pile dwellings on Swiss lakes. They did not yet have writing, so this period counts as prehistory.
13989.m: While pyramids were built in Egypt, pile dwellers without writing lived in Switzerland.

13990.q: What did people in Mesopotamia usually write cuneiform on?
13990.e: The signs were pressed into damp clay. Dried or fired tablets last a very long time.
13990.m: Cuneiform was mainly pressed into clay tablets.

13991.e: A cut reed stylus was pressed into the soft clay. This made the typical wedge-shaped marks.
13991.m: Wedges were pressed into soft clay with a reed stylus.

a: Because the signs are made of wedge-shaped strokes
Because it was hammered into wood with wedges
Because it came from a king called Cuneus
13992.e: When you press the stylus into clay, it leaves a mark that looks like a small wedge; ‘cuneus’ is Latin for wedge. All the signs are made of such wedges.
13992.m: The signs of cuneiform are made of small wedges.

13993.q: How did cuneiform develop over time?
a: From picture signs to abstract signs
13993.e: At first the signs still showed recognisable pictures. Over time they became simplified and abstract and also stood for syllables.
13993.m: Cuneiform changed from picture signs to abstract signs.

13994.q: Roughly how long was cuneiform used?
13994.e: Cuneiform developed around 3300 BC. The last known texts date from the 1st century AD.
13994.m: Cuneiform was used for about three thousand years.

13995.q: Which languages was cuneiform used for?
a: Several languages, such as Sumerian and Akkadian
13995.e: Cuneiform was used for Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite, Old Persian and other languages. It was something like the script of the ancient Near East.

13996.q: What were the signs of cuneiform pressed into the soft clay with?
13996.e: The scribes pressed a cut reed into the damp clay. This made the wedge-shaped strokes that gave the script its name.
13996.m: Cuneiform was pressed into clay with a reed.

13997.q: Why have so many cuneiform tablets survived to this day?
a: Clay becomes very durable when fired or dried
They were always cast in gold
They were all kept in fridges
They were copied out again every year
13997.e: Dried clay survives for thousands of years in the ground, and fired clay even better. When libraries burned, the tablets were even hardened further.
13997.m: Clay tablets are so durable that they have survived for thousands of years.

13998.q: Which river was the lifeline of ancient Egypt?
13998.e: Almost all Egyptians lived on the narrow, fertile strip along the Nile. All around was desert.
13998.m: Without the Nile there would have been no ancient Egypt.

13999.q: Why was the yearly Nile flood so important for the Egyptians?
a: It brought fertile mud to the fields
It filled the pyramids with water
It brought gold from the mountains
13999.e: Every summer the Nile burst its banks. Afterwards fertile mud was left behind, which the farmers could sow seeds in.
13999.m: The Nile flood made Egypt's fields fertile.

14000.q: Which two parts of the country were united into one kingdom around 3100 BC?
14000.e: Upper Egypt lies in the south, upstream, and Lower Egypt in the north with the Nile Delta. Their union is seen as the beginning of the kingdom of the pharaohs.
14000.m: Around 3100 BC Upper and Lower Egypt were united.

14001.q: From which plant did the Egyptians make a paper-like writing material?
14001.e: Papyrus grew in the marshes along the Nile. Its stems were cut into strips, laid crosswise and pressed.
14001.m: The Egyptians made writing sheets from the papyrus plant.

14002.q: Why did the Egyptians mummify their dead?
a: The body was to be preserved for life after death
14002.e: The Egyptians believed in a life after death. For this the body had to be preserved as well as possible.
14002.m: Mummies were meant to preserve the body for life after death.

14003.q: Which god was worshipped in Egypt as ruler of the realm of the dead?
14003.e: Osiris was regarded as the god of the afterlife and rebirth. He was often shown with green skin and as a mummy.
14003.m: Osiris was the Egyptian god of the realm of the dead.

14004.q: What is the name of the sun god who was one of the most important gods in ancient Egypt?
14004.e: According to Egyptian belief, Ra (also written Re) travelled across the sky in a boat. Many pharaohs called themselves ‘Son of Ra’.
14004.m: Ra was the Egyptian sun god.

14005.q: Which god with a jackal's head was responsible for embalming?
14005.e: Anubis was shown as a jackal or as a man with a jackal's head. He was regarded as the protector of the dead and of mummification.
