14005.m: Anubis with the jackal's head protected the dead.

14006.q: In which Swiss city does a museum of antiquities show a well-known collection of Egyptian art?
14006.e: The Antikenmuseum Basel und Sammlung Ludwig has an important department on ancient Egypt. It is displayed in a hall of its own.
14006.m: In Switzerland you can see Egyptian art at the Antikenmuseum Basel.

14007.q: Whose almost untouched tomb did Howard Carter discover in the Valley of the Kings in 1922?
14007.e: The tomb of the young pharaoh Tutankhamun was full of treasure. Most famous of all is his golden death mask.
14007.m: In 1922 Howard Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun.

14008.q: Roughly how old was Tutankhamun when he died?
14008.e: Tutankhamun became pharaoh as a child and died after about ten years on the throne. So he was still very young.
14008.m: Tutankhamun died as a young man.

14010.q: Which pharaoh ruled for about 66 years and had the temples of Abu Simbel built?
14010.e: Ramesses II ruled for a very long time in the 13th century BC. The rock temples of Abu Simbel show huge statues of him.
14010.m: Ramesses II had the rock temples of Abu Simbel built.

14011.q: Which pharaoh wanted people to worship above all a single god, the sun disc Aten?
14011.e: In the 14th century BC, Akhenaten promoted the worship of the Aten and founded a new capital. After his death, people returned to the old gods.
14011.m: Akhenaten placed the sun god Aten above all other gods.

14012.q: Who was the famous wife of Akhenaten, whose painted bust is now in Berlin?
14012.e: The bust of Nefertiti was found in Amarna in 1912. It is on display in the Neues Museum in Berlin.
14012.m: The bust of Nefertiti is a famous work of art in Berlin.

14013.q: Who was the last ruler of independent Egypt before the Roman conquest in 30 BC?
14013.e: Cleopatra VII came from a family of Greek origin, the Ptolemies. After her death, Egypt became a Roman province.
14013.m: With Cleopatra VII the independent kingdom of the pharaohs ended.

14014.q: Which objects did the pharaoh often hold in his hands as a symbol of his power?
14014.e: The crook was like a shepherd's staff and the flail like a fly whisk. They showed that the pharaoh led and protected his people.
14014.m: The crook and flail were signs of the pharaoh's power.

14015.q: What were the great pyramids in Egypt built for?
14015.e: The pyramids were enormous royal tombs. They were meant to secure the pharaoh's way into the afterlife.
14015.m: The pyramids were the tombs of the pharaohs.

14016.q: Which pharaoh had the largest pyramid at Giza built?
14016.e: The Great Pyramid of Khufu was built around 2600 BC. It is the largest pyramid in Egypt.
14016.m: The largest pyramid at Giza belongs to the pharaoh Khufu.

14017.q: Roughly how tall was the Great Pyramid of Khufu originally?
14017.e: Originally the Great Pyramid of Khufu was about 146 metres tall. Because the tip and the outer casing are missing, it is about 139 metres tall today.
14017.m: The Great Pyramid of Khufu was originally about 146 metres tall.

14019.q: Which pyramid is considered the oldest large pyramid in Egypt?
14019.e: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara was built around 2700 to 2650 BC. It consists of six steps stacked on top of each other.
14019.m: The Step Pyramid of Djoser is the oldest large pyramid.

14020.q: Which master builder designed the Step Pyramid of Djoser?
14020.e: Imhotep was a high official of the pharaoh Djoser. Later he was even worshipped as a god of healing.
14020.m: Imhotep is regarded as the builder of the first large pyramid.

14021.q: Which huge figure with a lion's body and a human head lies near the Pyramids of Giza?
14021.e: The Great Sphinx is carved out of the rock. It was probably made under the pharaoh Khafre, but this is not certain.
14021.m: The Great Sphinx of Giza has a lion's body and a human head.

14022.q: According to current research, who built the Pyramids of Giza?
a: Organised workers who were provided for
14022.e: Workers' villages and workers' tombs near Giza show that organised teams of workers built the pyramids. They received bread and beer as food, and many worked in shifts for a few months at a time.
14022.m: The pyramids were built by well-organised workers.

14023.q: On which side of the Nile are most pyramids?
a: On islands in the middle of the river
14023.e: The sun sets in the west. That is why the west was seen as the realm of the dead, and the tombs were built there.
14023.m: The pyramids are mostly west of the Nile, where the sun sets.

14024.q: What does the Greek word ‘hieroglyphs’ mean?
14024.e: ‘Hieros’ means sacred and ‘glyphein’ means to carve. The Greeks saw the signs mainly on temples and tombs.
14024.m: Hieroglyphs means something like sacred written signs.

14025.q: Which find helped to decipher hieroglyphs?
14025.e: The Rosetta Stone was found in Egypt in 1799. It carries the same text in three scripts.
14025.m: The Rosetta Stone was the key to hieroglyphs.

14026.q: Which three scripts are on the Rosetta Stone?
14026.e: Because scholars could read Greek, they could compare the other two versions of the text with it.
14026.m: The Rosetta Stone has one text in three scripts.

14027.e: The Frenchman Champollion realised that hieroglyphs can stand for both sounds and words. He presented his discovery in 1822.

14028.q: What is the oval frame in which the names of pharaohs were written called?
14028.e: The cartouche surrounds the royal name like a rope. During the decipherment, cartouches helped to recognise names such as Ptolemy and Cleopatra.
14028.m: A cartouche contains the name of a pharaoh.

a: Only letters as in the alphabet
14029.e: Some hieroglyphs stand for a word, others for one or more sounds. Determinatives showed which group a word belonged to.
14029.m: Hieroglyphs could represent words, sounds or hints.

14030.q: What was the simplified handwriting that Egyptian scribes used for everyday texts on papyrus called?
14030.e: Painting hieroglyphs took a long time. For letters and administration, scribes used the quicker handwriting called hieratic.
14030.m: For everyday use the Egyptians wrote a quicker handwriting.

14031.q: In which museum is the Rosetta Stone on display today?
14031.e: After the French were defeated in Egypt, the British took the stone in 1801. It has been on display in the British Museum since 1802.
14031.m: The Rosetta Stone is in the British Museum in London today.

14032.q: In which directions could hieroglyphs be written?
a: Right to left, left to right or top to bottom
14032.e: You can tell the reading direction by where the people and animals are looking. You read towards their faces.
14032.m: With hieroglyphs, the direction the figures face shows the reading direction.

14033.q: Which king founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire around 550 BC?
14033.e: Cyrus II, also called Cyrus the Great, defeated the Medes and built up a huge empire.
14033.m: Cyrus II founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

14034.q: In which present-day country was the Persian heartland?
14034.e: The Persians came from the region of Persis in the south-west of present-day Iran. From there they conquered a world empire.
14034.m: The heartland of the ancient Persians is in present-day Iran.

14035.q: How did the Persian kings govern their huge empire?
a: They divided it into provinces with governors
Each village elected its own king
The king visited every village himself
14035.e: The Persian Empire was divided into provinces. A governor, called a satrap, ran his province and collected taxes.
14035.m: The Persian Empire was divided into provinces with governors.

14036.q: What was the Persian Royal Road from Sardis to Susa used for?
a: Only as a pilgrims' way to temples
As a border wall against enemies
14036.e: The Royal Road was about 2700 kilometres long. Messengers took turns at stations with fresh horses and are said to have covered the distance in about nine days.
14036.m: The Royal Road linked the Persian Empire with a fast messenger service.

14037.q: Which magnificent royal city did Darius I have built?
14037.e: Persepolis was built from about 520 BC. Its ruins in Iran are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
14037.m: Persepolis was a magnificent residence of the Persian kings.

14038.q: How did the Persians under Cyrus II often treat the religions of conquered peoples?
a: They mostly let them keep their religion
They forced everyone into the Egyptian faith
14038.e: The Achaemenids generally tolerated the different religions in their empire. This helped to hold the huge empire together.
14038.m: The Persians often let conquered peoples keep their religion.

14039.q: Against whom did the Persians fight the Persian Wars in the 5th century BC?
14039.e: The Persians tried to conquer Greece. The Greeks won at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis in 480 BC.
14039.m: In the Persian Wars the Greeks fought against the Persian Empire.

14040.q: Who conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire around 330 BC?
14040.e: Alexander the Great of Macedonia defeated the Persian king Darius III. This was the end of the Achaemenid Empire.
14040.m: Alexander the Great ended the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

14041.q: Roughly how far did the Persian Empire stretch under Darius I?
14041.e: The Achaemenid Empire reached from Egypt and Asia Minor in the west to the Indus in the east. It was the largest empire of its time.
14041.m: The Persian Empire reached from Egypt to the Indus.

14042.q: On which coast did the Phoenicians live?
a: The eastern Mediterranean, in present-day Lebanon
14042.e: The Phoenicians lived in port cities on the coast of present-day Lebanon and Syria. The sea was their most important route.
14042.m: The Phoenicians lived on the coast of present-day Lebanon.

14043.q: What were the Phoenicians especially famous for?
14043.e: Phoenician traders sailed across the whole Mediterranean. They traded wood, glass, cloth and metals.
14043.m: The Phoenicians were skilled sailors and traders.

14044.q: Which important script did the Phoenicians develop, from which our alphabet later came?
14044.e: The Phoenician script had 22 signs, only for consonants. The Greeks took it over and added vowels, and later the Latin alphabet also came from it.
14044.m: Our alphabet goes back to the script of the Phoenicians.

14045.q: Which precious dye did the Phoenicians get from sea snails?
14045.e: You needed a huge number of snails for a little purple dye. That is why purple clothing was expensive and a sign of power.
14045.m: Expensive purple dye was made from sea snails.

14046.q: Which city in North Africa did the Phoenicians found, which later challenged Rome?
14046.e: Carthage lay in what is now Tunisia. According to tradition, it was founded in the 9th century BC by settlers from Tyre.
14046.m: Carthage was founded by the Phoenicians in North Africa.

14047.q: Which three cities were among the most important cities of the Phoenicians?
14047.e: Tyre, Sidon and Byblos were independent port cities. There was no single Phoenician empire.
14047.m: Tyre, Sidon and Byblos were important Phoenician port cities.

14048.q: Which valuable wood from their homeland did the Phoenicians sell to Egypt, among other places?
14048.e: Large cedar trees grew in the mountains of Lebanon. Their wood was in great demand for ships, palaces and temples.
14048.m: Cedar wood from Lebanon was an important Phoenician trade good.

14049.q: Where does the word “Bible” probably come from?
a: From the name of the Phoenician city of Byblos
14049.e: A lot of papyrus was traded through Byblos. So the Greeks called papyrus “byblos”, and this became “biblia” for books.
14049.m: The word Bible goes back to the port city of Byblos.

14050.q: Which former capital of the Assyrians lay on the Tigris in northern Mesopotamia?
14050.e: Nineveh lay opposite today's city of Mosul in Iraq. The great library of King Ashurbanipal was found there.
14050.m: Nineveh was an important Assyrian city on the Tigris.

14051.q: What is the name of the valley near Thebes where many pharaohs of the New Kingdom were buried?
14051.e: Instead of pyramids, people in the New Kingdom built tombs cut into the rock in the Valley of the Kings. They hoped this would protect them better from tomb robbers.
14051.m: Many pharaohs lie in rock tombs in the Valley of the Kings.

14052.q: How many great pyramids stand on the Giza plateau?
14052.e: On the plateau stand the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. There are also smaller pyramids for queens.
14052.m: Three great pyramids stand on the Giza plateau.

14053.q: What did the Persian king Darius I introduce to make trade and taxes easier?
14053.e: Darius I had the same gold coins minted throughout the empire. A single currency made trade and taxes simpler.
14053.m: Darius I introduced standard gold coins in the Persian Empire.

14054.q: What do you call an ancient Greek city-state?
14054.e: A Greek city-state was called a polis. It was made up of a city and the land around it, and it governed itself.
14054.m: A Greek city-state is called a polis.

14055.q: Why did many small, independent city-states develop in Greece instead of one large empire?
a: Mountains and sea separated the small plains from each other
The Greeks spoke many different languages
There were no rivers and no roads
14055.e: Greece is very mountainous and has many islands. The small fertile plains were cut off from each other, so separate communities developed there.
14055.m: The mountains of Greece encouraged many small city-states to form.

14056.q: Which word comes directly from the Greek term “polis”?
14056.e: The word politics comes from the Greek “polis”. It originally meant the affairs of the city and its citizens.
14056.m: The word politics comes from the Greek word polis.

14057.q: What was the central market and meeting place of a Greek city called?
14057.e: The agora was the centre of public life. People traded, discussed and held assemblies there.
14057.m: Citizens met in the agora to trade and discuss.

14058.q: What does the word “acropolis” literally mean?
14058.e: Acropolis means “upper city”. It refers to the fortified hill of a Greek city, where temples often stood.
14058.m: The acropolis was the fortified upper city on a hill.

14059.q: Roughly how many Greek city-states were there in the Classical period?
14059.e: In the Classical period there were about 700 poleis. Most were small and had only a few thousand inhabitants.
14059.m: There were hundreds of Greek city-states.

14060.q: Despite their independence, what did the Greek city-states have in common?
a: Language, gods and festivals like the Olympic Games
A shared army under one general
14060.e: Even though there were many city-states, the Greeks felt they were one people. They were united by the same language, belief in the same gods and shared festivals.
14060.m: Language, religion and festivals united the Greeks beyond their city borders.

14061.q: What did many Greek cities do between about 750 and 550 BC when land became too scarce?
a: They founded colonies on distant coasts
14061.e: In the period of the Great Colonisation, Greeks founded new cities around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, for example in southern Italy, Sicily and southern France.
14061.m: Greek settlers founded colonies around the Mediterranean.

14062.q: What do you call a form of rule in which a small group of rich or noble citizens governs?
14062.e: Oligarchy means “rule of the few”. In many city-states, only a few rich families decided on politics.
14062.m: In an oligarchy, a small group rules.

14063.q: What did the Greeks call a sole ruler who had seized power without any right of inheritance?
14063.e: For the Greeks, a tyrant was a ruler who had taken power without a lawful claim. The word was neutral at first and only later became negative.
14063.m: A tyrant took power without a lawful claim.

14064.q: What were the heavily armed foot soldiers of the Greek city-states called?
14064.e: Hoplites were citizens who bought their own armour with shield, helmet and spear. They fought in a tight battle line called the phalanx.
14064.m: The hoplites were the heavily armed citizen soldiers of Greece.

14065.q: To which goddess was the city of Athens dedicated?
14065.e: Athena was the protecting goddess of Athens. Her name and the name of the city are connected.
14065.m: Athena was the protecting goddess of Athens.

14066.q: Which famous temple stands on the Acropolis of Athens?
14066.e: The Parthenon was built in the 5th century BC for the goddess Athena. It is the best-known building on the Acropolis.
14066.m: The Parthenon on the Acropolis is the temple of Athena.

14067.q: Which statesman shaped Athens so strongly around the middle of the 5th century BC that people speak of an “age” named after him?
14067.e: Pericles led Athens around 450 BC. In his time great buildings were built and democracy was expanded.
14067.m: Under Pericles, Athens had its golden age.

14068.q: In which battle did the Athenians defeat the Persians in 490 BC?
14068.e: In 490 BC the Athenians defeated a Persian army at Marathon. Today's marathon race recalls a legend about a messenger who carried the news of victory to Athens.
14068.m: At Marathon the Athenians defeated the Persians in 490 BC.

14069.q: Which sea battle did the Greek fleet, led by Athens, win against the Persians in 480 BC?
14069.e: Near the island of Salamis the Greek fleet defeated the Persians in 480 BC. Before that, the Athenian Themistocles had pushed through the building of many warships.
14069.m: The sea battle of Salamis was a great Greek victory over the Persians.

14070.q: Which alliance did Athens lead after the Persian Wars?
14070.e: The Delian League, also called the Attic League, was founded in 478/477 BC. It made Athens the leading sea power.
14070.m: After the Persian Wars, Athens led the Delian League.

14071.q: What was the name of the main harbour of Athens, which was linked to the city by walls?
14071.e: Piraeus was the harbour of Athens. The so-called Long Walls protected the route between the city and the harbour.
14071.m: Piraeus was the great harbour of Athens.

14072.q: Which war between Athens and Sparta lasted from 431 to 404 BC?
14072.e: In the Peloponnesian War, Athens and Sparta and their allies fought for almost 30 years. In the end Sparta won.
14072.m: Athens lost to Sparta in the Peloponnesian War.

14073.q: Which art form was especially cultivated in ancient Athens at festivals for the god Dionysus?
14073.e: Tragedies and comedies were performed in the Theatre of Dionysus at the foot of the Acropolis. Famous writers were Sophocles and Aristophanes.
14073.m: Theatre began at the festivals for Dionysus in Athens.

14074.q: What badly weakened Athens shortly after the start of the Peloponnesian War and also cost Pericles his life?
14074.e: From 430 BC a terrible plague raged in the overcrowded city. Many people died, Pericles in 429 BC.
14074.m: A plague badly weakened Athens at the start of the Peloponnesian War.

14075.q: In which region of Greece is Athens?
14075.e: Athens lies on the Attica peninsula. That is where the term “Attic democracy”, for example, comes from.
14075.m: Athens is the most important city in the region of Attica.

14076.q: In which region of Greece was Sparta?
14076.e: Sparta lay in the south of the Peloponnese on the river Eurotas, in the region of Laconia.
14076.m: Sparta lay in the south of the Peloponnese.

14077.q: What was special about the way Sparta was governed?
a: It had two kings at the same time
The king was chosen by lot every year
14077.e: Sparta had two kings from two different families. Their main job was to lead the army.
14077.m: Sparta was led by two kings at the same time.

14078.q: Who in Sparta watched over the lives of the citizens and even the kings?
14078.e: Every year the assembly elected five overseers, the ephors. They had great power and even kept a check on the two kings.
14078.m: The ephors had great power in Sparta.

14079.q: Which men sat on the council of elders in Sparta?
14079.e: The council of elders was called the Gerousia. It was made up of 28 citizens over 60 and the two kings.
14079.m: Men over 60 sat on Sparta's council of elders.

14080.q: Who were the helots in Sparta?
a: Unfree people who had to farm the Spartans' land
14080.e: The helots were unfree people who worked the fields for the Spartan citizens. There were more of them than there were Spartans.
14080.m: The helots worked the Spartans' land as unfree people.

14081.q: At about what age did Spartan boys start their state education?
14081.e: At about 7 the boys left their families and lived in groups. This tough education was called the agoge and was meant to produce good soldiers.
14081.m: Spartan boys were raised by the state from about the age of seven.

14082.q: Which Spartan king fell with his 300 Spartans at Thermopylae in 480 BC?
14082.e: King Leonidas, with 300 Spartans and other Greeks, defended the narrow pass of Thermopylae against the Persians. He fell in the battle.
14082.m: Leonidas fought with 300 Spartans at Thermopylae.

14083.q: What were Sparta's laws known for?
a: Freedom never to become a soldier
14083.e: The Spartans traced their strict laws back to the legendary lawgiver Lycurgus. Citizens were to live simply and above all be good soldiers.
14083.m: Sparta's laws demanded a strict, simple life.

14084.q: What does it mean today if you express yourself “laconically”?
14084.e: The Spartans from Laconia were known for their short answers. That is why “laconic” today means using few words that hit the mark.
14084.m: Laconic means short and to the point.

14085.q: How was the life of girls in Sparta different from that in Athens?
a: They were never allowed to leave the house
They had to fight as soldiers
14085.e: In Sparta girls did sports such as running and wrestling so that they would have healthy children. In Athens, on the other hand, women mostly lived quietly at home.
14085.m: Spartan girls did sport, unlike the girls in Athens.

14086.q: How did Sparta lose its leading position in Greece in the 4th century BC?
14086.e: In 371 BC Thebes defeated the Spartan army at Leuctra. After that, Sparta lost a lot of land and its leading position.
14086.m: After its defeat by Thebes, Sparta began to decline.

14087.q: What does the Greek word “democracy” mean?
14087.e: Democracy is made up of “demos” for people and “kratos” for rule.
14087.m: Democracy means rule of the people.

14089.q: Where did the citizens of Athens decide together on laws, war and peace?
14089.e: In the assembly, in Greek the ekklesia, the citizens came together and voted. It met on the Pnyx hill.
14089.m: In the assembly, the citizens of Athens decided together.

14090.q: Who was NOT allowed to vote in Athenian democracy?
14090.e: Only adult male citizens could take part. Women, slaves and foreigners who had moved there, the metics, were excluded.
14090.m: In Athens only adult male citizens could take part.

14091.q: What was the job of the council in Athenian democracy?
a: It led the fleet in war
14091.e: The Council of 500 was made up of citizens chosen by lot. It prepared the topics and decisions for the assembly.
14091.m: The council prepared the decisions of the assembly.

14092.q: What did the Athenians write a politician's name on when voting in an ostracism?
14092.e: In an ostracism, citizens scratched a name onto a piece of broken pottery, in Greek an “ostrakon”. That is where the name comes from.
14092.m: In an ostracism, the Athenians voted with pieces of pottery.

14093.q: What happened to a politician who was voted out in an ostracism?
a: He had to leave the city for 10 years
He had to pay taxes for life
14093.e: Whoever got the most votes in an ostracism was banished for ten years. But he kept his property.
14093.m: Ostracism banished a politician for ten years.

14094.q: How were most officials and council members chosen in Athens?
14094.e: Most offices were filled by lot. This was meant to give every citizen a chance, so that the rich could not simply grab the offices.
14094.m: In Athens most offices were filled by lot.

14095.q: Which offices in Athens were not chosen by lot but by election, because they required a lot of skill?
14095.e: The ten generals, the strategoi, led the army and were elected every year. Pericles was elected general many times in a row.
14095.m: The generals of Athens were elected, not chosen by lot.

14096.q: Why did Pericles introduce daily allowances for jurors?
a: So that poorer citizens could take part too
So that the city collected more taxes
So that only the rich took on offices
So that soldiers were paid better
14096.e: Anyone serving as a juror could not work during that time. With the daily allowances, poorer citizens could also afford to take part.
14096.m: Daily allowances let poor citizens take part in politics too.

14097.q: What did Solon abolish in Athens around 594 BC?
14097.e: In the past, anyone who could not pay their debts became a slave. Solon ended this debt slavery and is seen as a pioneer of democracy.
14097.m: Solon abolished debt slavery in Athens.

14098.q: Which Swiss form of assembly today is most like the direct open-air voting of the Athenians?
14098.e: At a Landsgemeinde, voters vote directly in the open air. Today it still exists in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
14098.m: The Landsgemeinde is a form of direct democracy like in Athens.

14099.q: According to Greek belief, on which mountain did the most important gods live?
14099.e: The Greeks believed that the most important gods lived on Mount Olympus. It is the highest mountain in Greece.
14099.m: The Greek gods lived on Mount Olympus.

14101.q: Which realm did the god Poseidon rule over?
14101.e: Poseidon was the god of the sea. He carried a trident and was also thought to cause earthquakes.
14101.m: Poseidon was the god of the sea.

14102.q: Which god ruled over the underworld, the realm of the dead?
14102.e: Hades was the ruler of the underworld. That is why his realm itself was often called Hades.
14102.m: Hades ruled the realm of the dead.

14103.q: According to legend, which hero had to complete twelve difficult labours?
14103.e: Heracles, called Hercules by the Romans, had to complete twelve tasks, such as defeating the Nemean lion.
14103.m: In legend, Heracles completed twelve labours.

14104.q: In the legend, what trick did the Greeks use to capture the city of Troy?
a: A wooden horse full of warriors
14104.e: According to the legend, Greek warriors hid inside a large wooden horse. The Trojans brought it into the city, and at night the warriors opened the gates.
14104.m: In the legend, the Trojan Horse was a Greek trick.

14105.q: Which poet is said to have written the Iliad and the Odyssey?
14105.e: The Iliad tells of the Trojan War, the Odyssey of Odysseus's long wanderings. Both are attributed to Homer.
14105.m: Homer is seen as the poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey.

14106.q: According to legend, how long did Odysseus wander after the Trojan War?
14106.e: After ten years of war over Troy, Odysseus wandered for another ten years before he got home to Ithaca.
14106.m: Odysseus needed ten years for his journey home.

14107.q: According to legend, which Titan brought fire to humans and was punished for it?
14107.e: Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans. As punishment, Zeus had him chained to a rock.
14107.m: In legend, Prometheus brought fire to humans.

14108.q: According to legend, which monster lived in the labyrinth on Crete and was defeated by Theseus?
14108.e: The Minotaur was half man, half bull. With the help of Ariadne's thread, Theseus found his way back out of the labyrinth.
14108.m: In legend, Theseus defeated the Minotaur in the labyrinth.

14109.q: Where does the expression “Achilles heel” for a weak spot come from?
a: From the hero Achilles, who could only be wounded in the heel
From a running injury at Olympia
14109.e: According to legend, Achilles's mother dipped him in the river Styx but held him by the heel. Only there could he be hurt.
14109.m: An Achilles heel is a weak spot.

14110.q: In honour of which god were the ancient Olympic Games held?
14110.e: The games at Olympia were a religious festival for Zeus. A large temple of Zeus stood there.
14110.m: The ancient Olympic Games honoured the god Zeus.

14111.q: From which year do the recorded lists of Olympic winners begin?
14111.e: According to tradition, the first games took place in 776 BC. The lists of winners begin with this year.
14111.m: According to tradition, the Olympic Games began in 776 BC.

14112.q: How often were the ancient Olympic Games held?
14112.e: The games took place every four years. The time in between was called an Olympiad and was even used to count the years.
14112.m: The Olympic Games took place every four years.

14113.q: What did a winner at Olympia receive as a prize?
14113.e: The winner got a wreath from the wild olive tree. In his home city he was often richly rewarded and honoured as well.
14113.m: Olympic winners received an olive wreath.

14114.q: Roughly how long was the running track in the stadium at Olympia?
14114.e: The track at Olympia was about 192 metres long. This measure was called a stadion, which is where our word for the sports ground comes from.
14114.m: The word stadium originally meant a running distance of about 192 metres.

14115.q: What was the ancient five-event contest at Olympia called?
14115.e: The pentathlon was made up of discus, long jump, javelin, a sprint and wrestling.
14115.m: The pentathlon was the five-event contest of the ancient games.

14116.q: What was the pankration at Olympia?
a: A tough fight mixing wrestling and boxing
A chariot race with four horses
14116.e: The pankration was a combat sport that combined wrestling and boxing. Only biting and gouging eyes were forbidden.
14116.m: The pankration combined wrestling and boxing.

14117.q: In ancient times, what was the Olympic truce meant to ensure?
a: Safe travel for participants to Olympia
The end of all wars for ever
14117.e: During the Olympic truce, the ekecheiria, the athletes above all were to be able to travel to Olympia and stay there undisturbed.
14117.m: The Olympic truce protected journeys to Olympia.

14118.q: In ancient times, which group was not allowed to watch the games at Olympia?
14118.e: Married women were not allowed to watch. Women had their own races, the Heraia, in honour of the goddess Hera.
14118.m: Married women were not allowed to attend the ancient games.

14119.q: Why did the ancient Olympic Games end around AD 394?
a: A Christian emperor banned pagan festivals
An earthquake destroyed all of Greece
The Romans did not like sport
14119.e: Emperor Theodosius I banned the festivals for the old gods. The games at Olympia were a festival for Zeus.
14119.m: The ancient games ended because pagan festivals were banned.

14120.q: In which Swiss city is the International Olympic Committee based today?
14120.e: Pierre de Coubertin revived the games in Athens in 1896. The International Olympic Committee has its headquarters in Lausanne.
14120.m: The International Olympic Committee is based in Lausanne.

14121.q: What does the Greek word “philosophy” literally mean?
14121.e: Philosophy comes from “philos” for friend or love and “sophia” for wisdom.

14122.q: Which pupil of Socrates founded the Academy in Athens?
14122.e: Plato founded the Academy in Athens around 387 BC. It is seen as one of the first institutions of higher learning.
14122.m: Plato founded the Academy in Athens.

14123.q: Which philosopher was a pupil of Plato and the teacher of Alexander the Great?
14123.e: Aristotle studied with Plato for about 20 years. After that he taught the young Alexander and later founded his own school in Athens.
14123.m: Aristotle was the teacher of Alexander the Great.

14124.q: Which philosopher from Miletus is often seen as the first Greek philosopher?
14124.e: Thales of Miletus lived around 600 BC. He was one of the first to look for natural explanations of the world instead of just stories about gods.
14124.m: Thales of Miletus is seen as the first Greek philosopher.

14125.q: Which Greek thinker is a well-known theorem about right-angled triangles named after?
14125.e: Pythagoras' theorem describes the relationship between the sides of a right-angled triangle. It is named after Pythagoras but was already known earlier, for example in Babylon.
14125.m: Pythagoras' theorem is named after a Greek thinker.

14126.q: Which philosopher taught that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles?
14126.e: Democritus called these smallest particles “atomos”, which means indivisible. That is where our word atom comes from.
14126.m: Democritus imagined the world built from tiny particles, atoms.

14127.q: Which philosopher is said to have lived in a large clay jar out of modesty?
14127.e: Diogenes rejected wealth and luxury. According to tradition he lived in a large storage jar, often described as a barrel or tub.
14127.m: Diogenes is said to have lived in a clay jar.

14128.q: Which famous allegory by Plato describes people who only see shadows on a wall?
14128.e: In the Allegory of the Cave, chained people think shadows are reality. Plato uses it to show how hard the path to true knowledge is.
14128.m: Plato's Allegory of the Cave is about the path to true knowledge.

14129.q: What do people mean today when someone stays “stoically” calm?
a: They stay calm even when something bad happens
They do not speak a word of Greek
They never move from the spot
14129.e: The word comes from the Stoics, a school of philosophers in Athens. They taught people to bear blows of fate calmly.
14129.m: If you stay stoic, you accept difficult things calmly.

14130.q: What did the Greek philosopher Heraclitus mean by the saying “Everything flows”?
a: All water flows into the sea
14130.e: Heraclitus taught that nothing stays the same. A well-known image is that you cannot step into the same river twice.
14130.m: “Everything flows” means everything is constantly changing.

14131.q: Which Greek philosopher wrote no books himself, so that we know his teachings mainly from his pupil Plato?
14131.e: Socrates held discussions in the streets of Athens and asked lots of questions. It was his pupil Plato who wrote down his conversations.
14131.m: We know Socrates' teachings mainly through Plato.

14132.q: In which city did Socrates live and teach?
14132.e: Socrates was born in Athens around 469 BC and spent almost his whole life there.

14133.q: How many books did Socrates write himself?
14133.e: Socrates wrote nothing down. We know his ideas only from what others reported.
14133.m: Socrates left no writings of his own.

14134.q: Which pupil is the most important source for the conversations of Socrates?
14134.e: Plato wrote many dialogues in which Socrates is the main character. How accurately they show the real Socrates is debated.
14134.m: Plato's dialogues are the most important source on Socrates.

14135.q: How did Socrates get other people to think?
a: He gave long lectures without a break
He gave them tests with marks
14135.e: Socrates held conversations in the agora and asked questions until the people he was talking to realised what they really knew and what they did not.
14135.m: Socrates got people thinking by asking questions.

14136.q: Inspired by his mother's job, which art did Socrates compare his way of conversation to?
14136.e: His mother was a midwife. Socrates said he helped others to bring their own insights into the world. This method is called maieutics.
14136.m: Socrates called his method of conversation midwifery.

14137.q: Which well-known saying is often attributed to Socrates in a simplified form?
a: I know that I know nothing
I came, I saw, I conquered
14137.e: The saying expresses that Socrates was aware of what he did not know. In this form it greatly simplifies his attitude.
14137.m: Socrates was aware of how little he really knew.

14138.q: What did the Oracle of Delphi answer when asked whether anyone was wiser than Socrates?
14138.e: A friend of Socrates asked the oracle, and the answer was that nobody was wiser. Socrates then tested whether others really knew more.
14138.m: The Oracle of Delphi called Socrates the wisest.

14139.q: What was Socrates accused of at his trial?
a: Corrupting the young and disrespecting the gods
Stealing money from the state treasury
14139.e: Socrates was charged with corrupting the young and not honouring the city's gods. A court with about 500 jurors found him guilty.
14139.m: Socrates was charged with impiety and corrupting the young.

14140.e: Socrates lived in Athens from about 469 to 399 BC. That is about 2400 years ago.

14141.q: How was the death sentence against Socrates carried out?
a: He had to drink a cup of poison
He was thrown off a cliff
He was drowned in the sea
He was sent into the arena
14141.e: Socrates drank hemlock, a drink made from the poisonous hemlock plant. Plato describes his last hours in the dialogue “Phaedo”.

14142.q: Why did Socrates not escape from prison, even though friends wanted to help him?
a: He did not want to break the laws of his city
He was too ill to walk
The prison was unguarded but too far away
He wanted to wait for a king
14142.e: In Plato's dialogue “Crito”, Socrates explains that he wants to stay loyal to the laws of Athens, even if the verdict is unjust.
14142.m: Socrates stayed loyal to the laws of Athens until his death.

14143.q: Which kingdom did Alexander the Great come from?
14143.e: Alexander was born in 356 BC in Pella, the capital of Macedonia. Macedonia lay in the north of Greece.
14143.m: Alexander the Great came from Macedonia.

14144.q: Who was the father of Alexander the Great?
14144.e: Philip II made Macedonia the strongest power in Greece. After he was murdered in 336 BC, Alexander became king at the age of 20.
14144.m: Alexander's father was King Philip II of Macedonia.

14145.q: What was the name of Alexander the Great's famous horse?
14145.e: According to tradition, Alexander tamed the wild horse Bucephalus when he was still a boy. It went with him on his campaigns.
14145.m: Alexander's favourite horse was called Bucephalus.

14146.q: Against which great empire did Alexander go to war from 334 BC?
14146.e: In 334 BC Alexander crossed the Hellespont and attacked the Persian Empire. He won his first great victory at the river Granicus.

14147.q: In which battle did Alexander first defeat the Persian king Darius III in 333 BC?
14147.e: Alexander won at Issus in the south-east of Asia Minor in 333 BC. Darius III fled the battlefield. In German, many people know the memory rhyme “333, bei Issos Keilerei”.
14147.m: At Issus, Alexander defeated the Persian king in 333 BC.

14148.q: According to legend, what did Alexander do with the Gordian Knot?
a: He cut through it with his sword
He patiently untied it with his fingers
He gave it to the Persian king
14148.e: Whoever untied the complicated knot in Gordium was supposed to rule Asia. Alexander is said to have simply cut it with his sword.
14148.m: To cut the Gordian knot means to solve a difficult problem boldly.

14149.q: Which famous city did Alexander found in Egypt around 331 BC?
14149.e: Alexandria on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt became one of the largest cities of the ancient world. It was famous for its library and its lighthouse.
14149.m: Alexander founded the city of Alexandria in Egypt.

14150.q: How far east did Alexander lead his army before his soldiers forced him to turn back in 326 BC?
14150.e: Alexander marched as far as the rivers in today's Pakistan and northern India. At the river Hyphasis his exhausted soldiers refused to go any further.
14150.m: Alexander's campaign reached as far as India.

14151.q: Where did Alexander the Great die in 323 BC?
14151.e: Alexander died in 323 BC in Babylon, in today's Iraq. He was only about 32 years old.
14151.m: Alexander the Great died in Babylon in 323 BC.

14152.q: What happened to Alexander the Great's empire after his death?
a: His generals divided it among themselves
His son ruled it for 50 years
The Romans took it over at once
14152.e: Alexander died young and without a settled successor. His generals, the Diadochi, fought for decades over his legacy and divided up the empire.
14152.m: After Alexander's death his generals divided up the empire.

14153.q: What is the period after Alexander called, when Greek culture and language spread far to the east?
14153.e: Through Alexander's conquests, Greek culture spread from Egypt to Central Asia. This time is called the Hellenistic period, after “Hellenes”, as the Greeks called themselves.
14153.m: In the Hellenistic period, Greek culture spread across the whole East.

14154.q: Which year of Rome's founding does Roman tradition give?
14154.e: According to Roman legend, Rome was founded in 753 BC. The Romans sometimes counted their years “from the founding of the city”.
14154.m: Legend places the founding of Rome in 753 BC.

14155.q: According to legend, which twins founded Rome?
14155.e: According to legend, Romulus founded the city of Rome after killing his brother Remus in a quarrel. The city is said to be named after him.
14155.m: Romulus and Remus are the legendary founders of Rome.

14156.q: According to legend, which animal fed the abandoned twins who are said to have later founded Rome?
14156.e: The legend says that a she-wolf found the twins on the bank of the Tiber and fed them with her milk. The “Capitoline Wolf” is still a symbol of Rome today.
14156.m: The she-wolf with the twins is a symbol of Rome.

14157.q: On which river is the city of Rome?
14157.e: Rome grew up at a crossing point on the Tiber in central Italy. The river was important for trade and transport.
14157.m: Rome lies on the river Tiber.

14158.q: According to tradition, on how many hills was Rome built?
14158.e: Rome is traditionally called the “city of seven hills”. They include, for example, the Capitoline and the Aventine.
14158.m: Rome is known as the city of seven hills.

14159.q: According to legend, on which hill was the first settlement of Rome built?
14159.e: The Palatine is seen as the site of the first settlement. Archaeologists have actually found remains of very old huts there.
14159.m: The Palatine is seen as Rome's oldest settled hill.

14160.q: What did Rome become after the Romans drove out their last king?
14160.e: According to tradition, the Romans drove out their last king around 509 BC. After that, elected officials and the Senate governed. This form of state is called a republic.
14160.m: After the age of kings, Rome became a republic.

14161.q: Which people from central Italy strongly influenced early Rome before the Republic began?
14161.e: The Etruscans lived north of Rome and, according to tradition, provided Rome's last kings. The Romans took over a lot from them, for example in building and religion.
14161.m: The Etruscans had a great influence on early Rome.

14162.q: According to tradition, in which year did Rome become a republic?
14162.e: After the last king was driven out, the Republic began, according to tradition, in 509 BC. It lasted almost 500 years.
14162.m: According to tradition, the Roman Republic began in 509 BC.

14163.q: How many consuls led the state at the same time in the Roman Republic?
14163.e: As a rule there were two consuls, who kept a check on each other. This was meant to stop any one person from getting too much power.
14163.m: Two consuls led the Roman Republic together.

14164.q: For how long were consuls elected in the Roman Republic?
14164.e: The consuls' term of office lasted only one year. The short term was meant to prevent abuse of power.
14164.m: Roman consuls governed for only one year at a time.

14165.q: What was the name of the assembly of experienced men that had great influence on politics in Rome?
14165.e: The Senate was made up of former officials and mostly noble men. It advised the consuls and decided above all on foreign policy and finances.
14165.m: The Senate was Rome's most important advisory body.

14166.q: In the Roman Republic, what were the common people called, as opposed to the nobility?
14166.e: The patricians were the old noble families, the plebeians the common people. In the Conflict of the Orders, the plebeians fought for more rights.
14166.m: The plebeians fought for a long time for the same rights as the patricians.

14167.q: Which office in the Roman Republic protected the plebeians from unfair actions by officials?
14167.e: With his objection, the “veto”, the tribune could stop decisions against the plebeians. In Latin, “veto” means “I forbid”.
14167.m: The tribune could protect the plebeians with his veto.

14168.q: Against which city in North Africa did Rome fight the three Punic Wars?
14168.e: Rome and Carthage fought for control of the western Mediterranean. In 146 BC the Romans destroyed Carthage.
14168.m: In the Punic Wars, Rome defeated the city of Carthage.

14169.q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants to attack Rome?
14169.e: In the Second Punic War in 218 BC, Hannibal marched over the Alps into Italy with his army and elephants. In the end, Rome still won the war.
14169.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps into Italy with elephants.

14170.q: What was the largest unit of the Roman army, with several thousand soldiers, called?
14170.e: A legion usually had about 5000 to 6000 soldiers. It was divided into smaller units, the cohorts.
14170.m: A Roman legion had several thousand soldiers.

14172.q: What is the battle formation called in which legionaries held their shields together to form a closed shell?
14172.e: In the “tortoise”, in Latin testudo, the shields protected the soldiers from the front, the sides and above. This let them get close to walls without being hit by arrows.
14172.m: In the tortoise, legionaries protected themselves all round with their shields.

14173.q: What was the short sword of the Roman legionaries called?
14173.e: The gladius was a short sword for close combat. The pilum was the throwing spear, the scutum the large shield.
14173.m: The gladius was the short sword of the legionaries.

14174.q: Where was the Roman legionary camp on the territory of today's Switzerland?
14174.e: In the legionary camp of Vindonissa, in today's canton of Aargau, three legions were stationed one after another from AD 14 to 101. It lay at an important spot where the Aare and Reuss meet, close to where the Limmat flows in.
14174.m: Vindonissa near Windisch was the Roman legionary camp in Switzerland.

14175.q: What is the fortified border of the Roman Empire called, for example in Germania?
14175.e: The limes was a border defence with earth banks, wooden fences, watchtowers and forts. Parts of it are UNESCO World Heritage today.
14175.m: The limes protected the border of the Roman Empire.

14176.q: In which battle in AD 9 did the Romans lose three legions to Germanic tribes?
14176.e: In this battle, Germanic tribes under Arminius defeated the legions of Varus. In the years that followed, the Romans gave up their plans to rule Germania as far as the Elbe.
14176.m: In the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9, Rome lost three legions.

14177.q: What did auxiliary soldiers who were not Romans receive after their long service?
14177.e: The auxiliary troops were made up of men from the provinces. After about 25 years of service, they received Roman citizenship.
14177.m: Auxiliary soldiers received Roman citizenship after their service.

14178.q: Which large area did Julius Caesar conquer between 58 and 51 BC?
14178.e: In the Gallic War, Caesar conquered the area of today's France, Belgium and parts of Switzerland. He wrote a book about it himself.
14178.m: Caesar conquered all of Gaul in the Gallic War.

14180.q: Which border river did Caesar cross with his troops in 49 BC, starting a civil war?
14180.e: A general was not allowed to cross the Rubicon towards Rome with his army. Caesar did it anyway, and so began the civil war against Pompey.
14180.m: By crossing the Rubicon, Caesar started a civil war.

14181.q: Which famous saying is attributed to Caesar when he started the civil war in 49 BC?
a: I came, I saw, I conquered
14181.e: In Latin the saying is “Alea iacta est”. It means that a decision can no longer be undone.
14181.m: The saying “The die is cast” is attributed to Caesar.

14182.q: On which day was Julius Caesar murdered?
14182.e: Caesar was stabbed to death by a group of senators during a meeting of the Senate on the Ides of March 44 BC. They feared he wanted to rule like a king.
14182.m: Caesar was murdered on the Ides of March 44 BC.

14183.q: Which senator was one of the best-known murderers of Caesar?
14183.e: Marcus Junius Brutus was one of the leaders of the plot, even though Caesar had supported him. However, the famous words “You too, my son Brutus?” are not reliably recorded.
14183.m: Brutus was one of the leaders of the plot against Caesar.

14184.q: Which calendar goes back to a reform by Julius Caesar?
14184.e: The Julian calendar, with 365 days and a leap year every four years, was used from 45 BC. Much later it was improved by the Gregorian calendar.
14184.m: Caesar introduced the Julian calendar with leap years.

14185.q: By what name was Augustus known before he became emperor?
14185.e: Augustus was originally called Gaius Octavius. Later he was called Octavian, and he only received the honorary title “Augustus” from the Senate.
14185.m: Before becoming emperor, Augustus was called Octavian.

14186.q: How was Augustus related to Julius Caesar?
a: He was his great-nephew and adopted son
14186.e: Caesar was Octavian's great-uncle and named him in his will as his adopted son and heir. This helped Octavian win supporters.
14186.m: Augustus was Caesar's adopted son and heir.

14187.q: Whom did Octavian defeat in the sea battle of Actium in 31 BC?
14187.e: In the sea battle of Actium in Greece, Octavian defeated Mark Antony and the Egyptian queen Cleopatra. After that, Egypt became a Roman province.
14187.m: At Actium, Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra.

14188.q: What does the honorary name “Augustus” mean?
14188.e: In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian the title “Augustus”, which means “the exalted one”. This marked the start of the Roman imperial age.

14189.q: What did Augustus call himself so that he would not look like a king?
14189.e: Augustus did not want to appear like a king, because the Romans rejected kings. He called himself “princeps”, meaning first citizen, but he held the real power.
14189.m: Augustus called himself princeps, the first citizen.

14190.q: What is the long period of peace that began under Augustus called?
14190.e: After the many civil wars, Augustus brought a long time of peace within the empire. This time is called the Pax Augusta or Pax Romana.
14190.m: A long period of peace in the empire began under Augustus.

14191.q: Which month was named after Emperor Augustus?
14191.e: The month Sextilis was renamed “Augustus” in honour of Augustus. This became our month of August.
14191.m: The month of August is named after Emperor Augustus.

14192.q: Which area of today's Switzerland did Augustus have his stepsons conquer in 15 BC?
14192.e: In the Alpine campaign of 15 BC, Drusus and Tiberius conquered the Alpine regions. By then at the latest, the whole area of today's Switzerland came under Roman rule.
14192.m: In the Alpine campaign of 15 BC, Rome conquered the Alpine region.

14193.q: Under which emperor did a large part of Rome burn in AD 64?
14193.e: In the Great Fire of Rome, whole districts of the city were destroyed. According to the historian Tacitus, Nero then blamed the Christians.
14193.m: Under Emperor Nero, a large part of Rome burned in AD 64.

14194.q: Which city was buried when Vesuvius erupted in AD 79?
14194.e: Ash and pumice buried Pompeii. Today the excavations show in great detail how people lived back then.
14194.m: Pompeii was buried by Vesuvius in AD 79.

14195.q: Under which emperor did the Roman Empire reach its greatest size around AD 117?
14195.e: Under Emperor Trajan the empire stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia. It was never so large again.
14195.m: The Roman Empire was at its largest under Trajan.

14196.q: Which emperor had a long border wall built in Britain?
14196.e: Hadrian's Wall in the north of England was meant to protect the province of Britannia. It is about 117 kilometres long and is UNESCO World Heritage today.
14196.m: Emperor Hadrian had a border wall built in Britain.

14197.q: What were Roman aqueducts used for?
a: They carried water into the cities
14197.e: Aqueducts were water channels, often with bridges across valleys. They brought fresh water into the cities for fountains and baths.
14197.m: Roman aqueducts brought water into the cities.

14198.e: In the thermae, the Romans bathed in cold, lukewarm and warm water. They also met there to chat and do sport.
14198.m: Thermae were popular Roman public baths.

14199.q: Which of today's languages in Switzerland come from the Latin of the Romans?
14199.e: French, Italian and Romansh are Romance languages and developed from Latin. German is a Germanic language.
14199.m: Three of Switzerland's national languages come from Latin.

14200.q: Which city was inaugurated in AD 330 as the new capital in the east of the Roman Empire?
14200.e: The city was previously called Byzantion and was named after the emperor who had it expanded. Today it is called Istanbul.
14200.m: Constantinople, today's Istanbul, became the capital in AD 330.

14202.q: What is the name of the largest amphitheatre in Rome, which was opened in AD 80?
14202.e: The Colosseum, properly the Flavian Amphitheatre, held about 50,000 spectators. Gladiator fights and animal hunts took place there.
14202.m: In the Colosseum in Rome, gladiators fought in front of tens of thousands of spectators.

14203.q: Which gladiator led a great revolt against Rome from 73 to 71 BC?
14203.e: Spartacus was a gladiator from Thrace. With tens of thousands of slaves he fought against Roman armies until the revolt was crushed.
14203.m: Spartacus led the largest slave revolt against Rome.

14204.q: What weapons did a retiarius fight with?
a: A sword and a large shield
14204.e: The retiarius wore hardly any armour and tried to catch his opponent with the net. He was fast and agile.
14204.m: The retiarius fought with a net and a trident.

a: Slaves, prisoners of war and convicts
14205.e: Most gladiators were unfree people who were trained in gladiator schools. But there were also volunteers who hoped for fame and money.

14206.q: What did a gladiator receive as a sign that he no longer had to fight in the arena?
14206.e: The wooden sword or wooden staff was called a “rudis”. Whoever received it was released from fighting in the arena.
14206.m: With the wooden sword, a gladiator was released from the arena.

14207.q: What do you call the sand-covered fighting area in an amphitheatre?
14207.e: “Arena” means sand in Latin. The sand soaked up blood and gave the fighters a firm footing.
14207.m: The arena gets its name from the Latin word for sand.

14208.q: How did most people in the Roman Empire become slaves?
14208.e: During conquests the Romans captured many people and sold them at slave markets. Pirates and human traffickers also sold captives.
14208.m: Many slaves in the Roman Empire were prisoners of war.

14209.q: What was the legal status of slaves in the Roman Empire?
a: They were seen as the property of their owners
They were citizens with the right to vote
14209.e: Slaves had hardly any rights and could be sold. How well or badly they were treated depended a lot on their owner and their work.
14209.m: Roman slaves were seen as property and had hardly any rights.

14210.q: How could a slave in the Roman Empire sometimes gain their freedom?
a: By being freed, often in return for payment
14210.e: Owners could free slaves, sometimes only in their will. Some slaves bought their freedom with their savings and were then called freedmen, in Latin liberti.
14210.m: Roman slaves could be freed or buy their freedom.

14211.q: Where did slaves in the Roman Empire have to work in especially harsh conditions?
14211.e: In mines and quarries the work was hard and dangerous. Many slaves died young there.
14211.m: Work in the mines was especially hard for slaves.

14212.q: What job did educated slaves, often from Greece, have in rich Roman families?
14212.e: Many private tutors in Rome were educated Greek slaves. They taught the children reading, writing and Greek.
14212.m: Educated slaves in Rome often worked as private tutors.

14213.q: At which festival in December were slaves in Rome allowed to celebrate almost like free people for a short time?
14213.e: During the Saturnalia the rules were relaxed for a few days. Masters and slaves sometimes ate together, and afterwards the old order applied again.
14213.m: During the Saturnalia the rules for slaves were briefly relaxed.

14214.q: What was the status of children of an enslaved woman in the Roman Empire?
14214.e: Under Roman law, a child's status followed the mother's. Children of an enslaved woman were therefore unfree from birth.
14214.m: In Rome, children of an enslaved woman were unfree from birth.

14215.q: According to the Gospels, under which Roman governor was Jesus crucified?
14215.e: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of the province of Judaea. According to the Gospels, he sentenced Jesus to death on the cross.
14215.m: Jesus was crucified under the governor Pontius Pilate.

14216.q: Which apostle spread Christianity on many journeys through the Roman Empire?
14216.e: Paul travelled through Asia Minor and Greece and founded Christian communities. His letters are in the New Testament.
14216.m: The apostle Paul spread Christianity in the Roman Empire.

14217.q: Why were Christians persecuted at times in the Roman Empire?
a: They refused to worship the emperor as a god
They did not want to pay taxes
14217.e: Christians believed in only one God and refused to make sacrifices for the emperor. This was seen as a danger to the state, so they were persecuted at times.
14217.m: Christians were persecuted because they rejected the worship of the emperor.

14218.q: Which emperor allowed Christians to practise their faith freely in AD 313 with the Edict of Milan?
14218.e: Constantine the Great and his co-emperor Licinius granted freedom to all religions. Christians could now practise their faith openly and got back property that had been seized.
14218.m: Emperor Constantine allowed the Christian faith in AD 313.

14219.q: What did Christianity become in the Roman Empire in AD 380?
14219.e: Emperor Theodosius I declared Christianity the official religion of the empire. Old cults were then banned bit by bit.
14219.m: In AD 380 Christianity became the state religion.

14220.q: Which animal is seen as an early symbol of the Christians?
14220.e: The Greek word for fish, “Ichthys”, was read as an abbreviation for “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour”. So the fish became a Christian symbol.
14220.m: The fish was an early symbol of the Christians.

14221.q: According to legend, who was Saint Maurice, after whom the town of Saint-Maurice in Valais is named?
14221.e: According to legend, Maurice was the leader of the Theban Legion. He and his soldiers died because, as Christians, they did not want to fight against Christians. Whether this really happened is not certain.
14221.m: According to legend, Saint Maurice was a Christian soldier.

14222.q: According to legend, which saints are the patron saints of Zurich?
14222.e: According to legend, Felix and Regula were executed in Zurich for being Christians. Whether they really lived is not certain.
14222.m: According to legend, Felix and Regula are the patron saints of Zurich.

14223.q: Which group of peoples did the Helvetii belong to?
14223.e: The Helvetii were a Celtic tribe in the Swiss Plateau. They lived in villages and fortified settlements called oppida.
14223.m: The Helvetii were a Celtic people.

14224.q: Who defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte in Gaul in 58 BC?
14224.e: The Helvetii wanted to move to south-western Gaul. Caesar stood in their way and defeated them at Bibracte.
14224.m: Caesar defeated the Helvetii at Bibracte in 58 BC.

14225.q: What did Caesar order the Helvetii to do after their defeat at Bibracte?
14225.e: Caesar sent the survivors back to their old area of settlement. That way the land would not stay empty and would not be taken over by Germanic tribes.
14225.m: After Bibracte, the Helvetii had to return to their homeland.

14226.q: Where did the Helvetii want to move to in 58 BC?
14226.e: The Helvetii burned their villages and wanted to move to south-western Gaul in today's France. Caesar stood in their way and defeated them at Bibracte.
14226.m: The Helvetii wanted to move to south-western Gaul.

14227.q: What does the abbreviation “CH” for Switzerland stand for?
14227.e: “Confoederatio Helvetica” is Latin and means “Helvetic Confederation”. The name recalls the Helvetii.
14227.m: The abbreviation CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.

14228.q: Against whom did the Helvetii win a great victory in 107 BC?
14228.e: The leader Divico and a group of Helvetii defeated a Roman army in south-western Gaul. Caesar later mentions this victory in his account.
14228.m: The Helvetii defeated a Roman army in 107 BC.

14229.q: What was today's city of Zurich called in Roman times?
14229.e: Turicum was a Roman customs post on the Limmat. A gravestone with this name was found on the Lindenhof in 1747.
14229.m: In Roman times Zurich was called Turicum.

14230.q: What was today's city of Geneva called in Roman times?
14230.e: Genava lay where the Rhône flows out of Lake Geneva. Caesar already mentions the place in his account of the Gallic War.
14230.m: In Roman times Geneva was called Genava.

14231.q: Near which of today's municipalities are the ruins of Augusta Raurica?
14231.e: Augusta Raurica lies east of Basel on the Rhine. Augst belongs to the canton of Basel-Landschaft, Kaiseraugst to the canton of Aargau.
14231.m: Augusta Raurica lies near Augst and Kaiseraugst.

14232.q: Which people founded the town of Augusta Raurica?
14232.e: Augusta Raurica was a Roman colony on the Rhine. The name honours Emperor Augustus and the Celtic tribe of the Rauraci.
14232.m: Augusta Raurica was a Roman town.

14233.q: Which people is Augusta Raurica named after?
14233.e: The Rauraci were a Celtic tribe in the area around Basel. “Augusta” also honours Emperor Augustus.
14233.m: Augusta Raurica bears the name of the Celtic tribe of the Rauraci.

14234.q: Roughly how many people lived in Augusta Raurica at its height?
14234.e: For its height around AD 200, experts estimate between about 10,000 and 20,000 inhabitants. That made it an important Roman town north of the Alps.
14234.m: At its height, Augusta Raurica probably had 10,000 to 20,000 inhabitants.

14235.q: Which famous find was discovered in Augusta Raurica in 1961 and 1962?
14235.e: The treasure includes about 270 objects made from about 58 kilograms of silver, such as plates, bowls and coins. It was buried around AD 350, but nobody knows for sure why.
14235.m: An important late Roman silver treasure was found in Augusta Raurica.

14236.q: Which large building in Augusta Raurica is still used for performances today?
14236.e: The Roman theatre of Augusta Raurica held several thousand spectators. It has been restored and is used again today as a venue for concerts and performances.
14236.m: Performances are held again today in the Roman theatre of Augusta Raurica.

14237.q: What did the Romans build right on the Rhine near Augusta Raurica around AD 300 to protect the border?
14237.e: After attacks and destruction in the 3rd century, the Castrum Rauracense was built right on the Rhine. It guarded the border against the Alemanni.
14237.m: The Castrum Rauracense guarded the Rhine border.

14238.q: What is the name of today's small town where the Roman town of Aventicum used to be?
14238.e: Avenches is in the canton of Vaud, near Lake Murten. Many remains of the Roman town can be seen there.
14238.m: The Roman town of Aventicum was at today's Avenches.

14239.q: What was the importance of Aventicum for the Helvetii in Roman times?
14239.e: Aventicum was the main town of the civitas of the Helvetii. The administration of the Helvetian territory was organised here.
14239.m: Aventicum was the main town of the Helvetii in Roman times.

14240.q: Which Roman building can still be clearly seen in Avenches today?
14240.e: The amphitheatre of Aventicum held thousands of spectators. Today concerts and festivals take place there again.
14240.m: The Roman amphitheatre still stands in Avenches.

14241.q: Which gold find was discovered in Aventicum in 1939?
a: A bust of Emperor Marcus Aurelius
14241.e: The golden bust of Marcus Aurelius was found in a drain near a temple. Today it is one of the best-known Roman finds in Switzerland.
14241.m: A golden bust of Marcus Aurelius was found in Aventicum in 1939.

14242.q: Roughly how long was the town wall of Aventicum?
14242.e: The town wall was a good 5 kilometres long and had 73 towers. It enclosed a much larger area than was actually lived in.
14242.m: The town wall of Aventicum was several kilometres long.

14243.q: Which bird is the tall Roman column “Cigognier” in Avenches named after?
14243.e: The French word for stork is “cigogne”. Storks used to nest on top of the temple column, which is about 12 metres high.
14243.m: The Cigognier is named after the storks that nested on the column.

14244.q: Next to which Roman building in Aventicum does the medieval tower with the Roman Museum stand?
14244.e: Above the main entrance of the amphitheatre stands a medieval tower that houses the Roman Museum. For a long time there was an opera festival in the amphitheatre; today there are concerts and festivals.
14244.m: The Roman Museum stands at the amphitheatre of Aventicum.

14245.q: In which year did the Western Roman Empire end with the removal of its last emperor?
14245.e: In this year, a Germanic military leader removed the last emperor in Italy and did not appoint a new one. This year is seen as the end of the Western Roman Empire.
14245.m: The Western Roman Empire ended in AD 476.

14246.q: What was the name of the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire?
14246.e: Romulus Augustulus was still a teenager when he was removed from power. His name recalls the city's founder Romulus and the first emperor Augustus.
14246.m: Romulus Augustulus was the last Western Roman emperor.

14247.q: Which Germanic military leader removed the last Western Roman emperor?
14247.e: Odoacer then took over rule in Italy himself. He sent the imperial insignia to the emperor in the Eastern Roman Empire.
14247.m: Odoacer removed the last Western Roman emperor.

14248.q: Into which two parts was the Roman Empire finally divided in AD 395?
14248.e: After the emperor's death, each of his two sons received one half of the empire. From then on, the Western and Eastern Empires developed separately.
14248.m: After 395 there was a Western Roman Empire and an Eastern Roman Empire.

14249.q: Which people under King Alaric plundered the city of Rome in AD 410?
14249.e: The plundering of Rome by the Visigoths shocked people throughout the empire. Rome had not been captured by enemies for about 800 years.
14249.m: The Visigoths under Alaric plundered Rome in AD 410.

14250.q: What are the great movements of Germanic and other peoples that weakened the Western Roman Empire called?
14250.e: From the late 4th century, many peoples pushed into the Roman Empire, partly because the Huns were driving them out of the east. The empire could hardly protect its borders any more.
14250.m: The Migration Period contributed to the fall of Western Rome.

14251.q: Which Germanic people settled mainly in northern and eastern Switzerland after the end of Roman rule?
14251.e: The Alemanni brought their Germanic language with them. Swiss German developed from it, while in western Switzerland the Burgundians took over the Latin language.
14251.m: The Alemanni shaped German-speaking Switzerland after Roman times.

14252.q: Until when did the Eastern Roman Empire continue?
14252.e: The Eastern Roman or Byzantine Empire outlived Western Rome by almost 1000 years. In 1453 the Ottomans conquered its capital.

14253.q: In which year was Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome?
14253.e: On Christmas Day in the year 800, Charles was crowned emperor by the Pope in Rome. This meant there was once again an emperor in the West, as in the old Roman Empire.
14253.m: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Rome in the year 800.

14254.e: Pope Leo III placed the imperial crown on Charles’s head in St Peter’s in Rome. Charles had earlier supported the Pope against opponents in Rome.
14254.m: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor.

14255.q: In which city did Charlemagne most like to stay in his later years?
14255.e: Charles had no fixed capital but travelled with his court from palace to palace. In his later years he mostly lived at the palace of Aachen, where he is also buried.

14256.q: Against which people did Charlemagne wage war for around 30 years?
14256.e: The Saxon Wars lasted from 772 to 804. Charles conquered the Saxons and forced them to accept Christianity.
14256.m: Charlemagne fought the Saxons for around 30 years.

14257.q: What were the envoys called whom Charlemagne used to check on the counts in his empire?
14257.e: The king’s envoys (in Latin missi dominici) usually travelled through the empire in pairs. They checked whether the counts followed the king’s orders and judged fairly.
14257.m: King’s envoys checked on the counts on Charles’s behalf.

14258.q: Which easy-to-read script developed in the time of Charlemagne?
14258.e: In the writing rooms of the Carolingian empire, Carolingian minuscule developed, with clear small letters. Our lower-case letters today go back to this script.
14258.m: Our lower-case letters come from Carolingian minuscule.

14259.q: According to a legend, what did Charlemagne found in Zurich?
14259.e: According to a legend, Charlemagne found the graves of the city’s saints Felix and Regula while hunting and founded the Grossmünster there. This story is not historically proven.
14259.m: According to legend, Charlemagne founded Zurich’s Grossmünster.

14260.q: Which Frankish king was baptised as a Christian around 500?
14260.e: The Merovingian Clovis I united the Franks and was baptised around 500. This made the Frankish kingdom a Christian kingdom.
14260.m: Clovis I made the Franks Christians.

14261.q: Which people, who also settled in today’s German-speaking Switzerland, were defeated by the Frankish king around 500?
14261.e: The Frankish king defeated the Alemanni around 496, and decisively again in 506. After that they gradually came under Frankish rule.
14261.m: Around 500, the Franks defeated the Alemanni.

14262.q: What office did Charles Martel and Pepin hold at the court of the Merovingian kings?
14262.e: The mayor of the palace originally ran the royal court. Over time, the mayors of the palace had more power than the Merovingian kings themselves.
14262.m: The mayors of the palace were the real rulers in the late Merovingian kingdom.

14263.q: Which Carolingian became the first of his family to be King of the Franks in 751?
14263.e: In 751, with the Pope’s approval, Pepin the Short removed the last Merovingian king. He was the father of Charlemagne.
14263.m: Pepin the Short was the first Carolingian king.

14264.q: Whom did Charles Martel fight in 732 at the Battle of Tours and Poitiers?
14264.e: In 732, Charles Martel defeated an Arab army that had pushed north from Spain. The Arabs withdrew, but smaller battles in the south of France went on for years.
14264.m: In 732, Charles Martel stopped an Arab army in the Frankish kingdom.

14265.q: What happened to the Frankish empire in the Treaty of Verdun in 843?
a: It was divided into three parts
14265.e: Charlemagne’s three grandsons divided the empire among themselves. The western part later became France, and the eastern part developed into what later became Germany.
14265.m: The Treaty of Verdun divided the Frankish empire into three parts in 843.

14266.q: Which region did the Vikings come from?
14266.e: The Vikings came from what is now Norway, Sweden and Denmark. This region is called Scandinavia.

14267.q: Which place was raided by Vikings in 793, an event seen as the start of the Viking Age?
14267.e: In 793, Vikings raided the monastery of Lindisfarne on the coast of England. This event is seen as the start of the Viking Age.
14267.m: The raid on Lindisfarne in 793 began the Viking Age.

14268.q: What are the fast, narrow ships of the Vikings called?
14268.e: Longships sat shallow in the water and could be sailed and rowed. That way the Vikings crossed the sea and also travelled up rivers.
14268.m: The Vikings travelled across seas and rivers in longships.

14269.q: Which Viking reached North America around the year 1000?
14269.e: Leif Erikson sailed from Greenland to North America and called the land Vinland. Remains of a Viking settlement have been found in Newfoundland.
14269.m: Leif Erikson reached America around 500 years before Columbus.

14270.q: Which region in France is named after the Vikings?
14270.e: In the year 911, the Viking leader Rollo received land on the Seine from the French king. The area was named Normandy after the “Northmen”.
14270.m: Normandy takes its name from the Northmen.

14271.q: Which god was the father of the gods in the Viking religion?
14271.e: The Vikings believed in many gods. Odin was seen as the father of the gods, and his son Thor as the god of thunder.
14271.m: Odin was the chief god of the Vikings.

14272.q: Which island in the North Atlantic did the Vikings settle from about 870 onwards?
14272.e: Settlers from Norway made their home in Iceland from about 870. There, in 930, the Althing was founded, one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
14272.m: From about 870, Vikings settled the island of Iceland.

14273.q: Which stages of training did a boy go through to become a knight?
14273.e: At about seven, a noble’s son went to another lord’s court as a page. At about 14 he became a knight’s squire, and usually at around 21 a knight himself.
14273.m: A future knight was first a page and then a squire.

14274.q: What was the solemn ceremony called in which a squire was admitted to knighthood?
14274.e: When he was girded with the sword, the squire received his sword and so became a knight. Later people also spoke of the accolade, or dubbing.
14274.m: Girding with the sword turned a squire into a knight.

14275.q: What were the fighting contests called in which knights showed their skill?
14275.e: At tournaments, knights fought each other on horseback with lances. They practised for war and could win fame and prizes.
14275.m: At tournaments, knights competed in combat.

14276.q: What were the knights’ coats of arms for?
14276.e: Under helmet and armour, knights could hardly be recognised. The coat of arms on the shield showed who was hidden underneath.
14276.m: You could recognise a knight in full armour by his coat of arms.

14277.q: What are the love songs called that knights performed for noble ladies at court?
14277.e: In Minnesang, poets sang of their devotion to a noble lady. It was part of the courtly culture of the age of knights.
14277.m: Minnesang was the courtly love poetry of the knights.

14278.q: What did knights’ protective clothing mainly consist of in the High Middle Ages?
14278.e: Chain mail was made of thousands of small iron rings. Full suits of armour made of iron plates only became common in the late Middle Ages, especially in the 15th century.
14278.m: In the High Middle Ages, knights mainly wore chain mail.

14279.q: Where did the Swiss Confederates defeat a Habsburg army of knights in 1315?
14279.e: At Morgarten, the Confederates ambushed the Habsburg army in a narrow pass. The heavily armoured knights could hardly defend themselves there.
14279.m: At Morgarten in 1315, the Confederates defeated Habsburg knights.

14280.q: What is the tallest and strongest tower of a castle called?
14280.e: The keep was usually the tallest tower of the castle. It served as a lookout and showed the lord’s power; it may also have been a last refuge during attacks.
14280.m: The keep was the main tower of a castle.

14281.q: What is the residential building with the knights’ hall in a castle called?
14281.e: The lord’s family lived in the palas. The great hall for feasts and receptions was also here.
14281.m: The lord’s family lived in the palas.

14283.q: What was a drawbridge at a castle for?
14283.e: The drawbridge led across the moat to the gate. When there was danger, it was pulled up so that attackers could not reach the gate.
14283.m: The drawbridge could block the way to the castle gate.

14284.q: In which present-day canton is Habsburg Castle, the ancestral seat of the Habsburgs?
14284.e: Habsburg Castle was built in the 11th century near Brugg, in what is now the canton of Aargau. The Habsburg family named itself after it.
14284.m: The ancestral castle of the Habsburgs is in Aargau.

14286.q: Why were many castles built on mountains or rocks?
14286.e: On high ground you could see enemies early, and attackers had to fight uphill. Such castles are called hilltop castles.
14286.m: Hilltop castles were especially well protected.

14287.q: What was a fief in the Middle Ages?
a: Land lent in return for loyalty and service
14287.e: A lord let a follower use land or rights. But the land still belonged to the lord.
14287.m: A fief was land granted in return for loyalty and service.

14288.q: What do you call someone who received a fief from a lord?
14288.e: The vassal was the one who held the fief, and the lord was called the liege lord. Both were bound by mutual loyalty.
14288.m: A vassal received a fief from his liege lord.

14289.q: Who was at the top of the feudal pyramid?
14289.e: The king granted fiefs to dukes, counts and bishops. They in turn passed parts of them on to lesser vassals.
14289.m: The king was at the top of the feudal pyramid.

14290.q: What did a vassal mainly have to provide for his lord?
a: Years of travel as a journeyman
14290.e: The vassal had to come to his lord’s aid with armed fighters. He also owed him advice and loyalty.
14290.m: Vassals mainly owed their lord military service.

14291.q: What did the liege lord promise his vassal in return for his loyalty?
a: Freedom from dues to the Church
14291.e: The feudal relationship was based on give and take. The lord gave land and protection, the vassal loyalty and service.
14291.m: The liege lord owed his vassal protection.

14292.q: How did fiefs change over the course of the Middle Ages?
14292.e: Originally a fief went back to the lord when the vassal died. Over time, however, the sons inherited the fief, which strengthened the power of the nobility.

14293.q: According to medieval thinking, which three estates of society were there?
14293.e: According to this idea, each of the three estates had its own task, willed by God. That is why people thought this order was right and could not be changed.
14293.m: Society was made up of clergy, nobility and peasants.

14294.q: According to the order of estates, what was the task of the nobility?
14294.e: The nobility was the estate of those who fight. It was meant to protect the other estates with weapons.
14294.m: The nobility had the task of protecting the others.

14295.q: In the Middle Ages, how did people usually become members of an estate?
